query:
Context: We operate a Nilfisk CFM 118EXP explosion-proof industrial vacuum in a university research lab
(BYU) to collect excess gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (aluminum-silicon-magnesium, ~20-63 um with sub-micron
fines) and elemental silicon powder from additive-manufacturing / ultrasonic-atomization research. The
unit is CSA Class I Group D / Class II Groups E,F,G. Its OEM 118EXP manual (UL 1213 par. 22, "TEST FOR
GROUND CONTINUITY BEFORE EACH USE") requires that the resistance of the grounding-continuity path
"shall not exceed 0.1 ohm," checked connection-by-connection (tool to wand, wand to hose, hose to
machine), and states "any alteration to this equipment by a third party will nullify its certification."
The manual's accessories BOM lists the crevice tool (P/N 01768900) with material = "Aluminium" (no
finish specified) and the hose as "Conductive." Prior Edison trajectories in this chain already covered
bag-vs-liner selection, emptying cadence, the powder-disposal SOP, and verification of the first-test-run
operating procedure (continuity acceptance targets, PPE, technique, sealing, cleaning).

We are doing pre-use ground-continuity testing before the first live powder run and hit an anomaly on
one attachment. Please VERIFY and interpret the following ACTUAL BENCH MEASUREMENTS against the
combustible-metal-dust / static-control literature and standards (NFPA 484, NFPA 652/654, NFPA 77,
UL 1213, OSHA 1910, ANSI/ESD, Aluminum Association, peer-reviewed dust-ignition/MIE and anodize/dielectric
literature). Meter: bench DMM accurate to ~0.01 ohm, REL used to null lead resistance (low-ohms range).

MEASUREMENTS (probes pressed firmly, large contact area, held still):
- Aluminum wand (01768601), tool-less: < 0.1 ohm end-to-end. Accessory coupler: < 0.1 ohm.
- Conductive antistatic hose: ~4 ohm end-to-end (manufacturer confirmed this is NORMAL for their
  conductive/flex hose; spec R <= 10^4 ohm).
- Vacuum body sections to each other ~0.2 ohm; lid-to-ground cable ~1 ohm.
- DUST BRUSH (01719401): tool-to-wand ~0.03 ohm — a clean, genuine metal-to-metal bond. PASSES.
- CREVICE TOOL (01768900), BRAND-NEW genuine Nilfisk part, unambiguously solid METAL (not plastic),
  the SAME silvery color as the low-resistance aluminum wand:
    * Surface-to-surface probing on the outer body: reads OL (over-range/open) on the REL-locked low
      range; with REL off and autoranging on, it climbs to MEGOHMS. So the outer skin behaves as an
      INSULATOR (~10^6 ohm class), roughly 10^5x over the < 10 ohm bonding target.
    * Probing AT THE JOINT where the crevice tool seats onto the wand: still OPEN — the tool does NOT
      bond to the wand through its socket as supplied.
    * Making LIGHT SCRATCHES in the surface and probing on/near the scratches: NO change, still open.
    * Nilfisk general technical customer support says the tool is "just aluminum," the rep did not know
      why it fails continuity, and referred us to their industrial-vacuum division (callback pending).

OUR WORKING HYPOTHESIS (please confirm, correct, or refute with citations): the crevice tool is
CLEAR/NATURAL ANODIZED aluminum — i.e., conductive aluminum bulk under a hard aluminum-oxide (Al2O3)
DIELECTRIC skin. That would explain: solid metal yet a persistent surface open; identical appearance to
the (also-aluminum) wand; a scratch that fails to restore continuity (anodize is Mohs ~9, harder than
the base metal, so a light scratch/probe-drag does not reach bright metal, and a low-voltage DMM at < ~3 V
cannot break down a coating that insulates to hundreds of volts). "Just aluminum" from Nilfisk names the
alloy, not the finish, and does not rule out anodize.

Please address, each with a CORRECT / CORRECT-WITH-CAVEAT / INCORRECT / UNSUPPORTED verdict and citations:

1. MEASUREMENT INTERPRETATION. Is the "OL on REL-locked range, megohms with autoranging" behavior a
   correct reading of a genuinely high (~10^6 ohm) surface resistance rather than a meter artifact? Is a
   persistent surface open that SURVIVES light scratching diagnostic of an engineered dielectric skin
   (anodize) as opposed to a few-nm native-oxide or machining-oil film (which ordinary probe pressure or
   a wipe defeats)? Give the expected surface resistivity / dielectric strength of sulfuric (clear)
   anodize and confirm a low-range ohmmeter cannot punch through it.

2. IS IT ANODIZED? From the physics + any available Nilfisk/industry sourcing or standard practice for
   aluminum vacuum tubes/nozzles, is clear anodize the most likely explanation for this exact symptom
   set (vs bare mill aluminum with native oxide, vs carbon-loaded "dissipative" plastic that merely looks
   metallic)? If you can find documentation of the 01768900 finish, report it; if the literature is
   silent, say so and give the most-likely conclusion.

3. IS AN ANODIZED EXP TOOL A DEFECT / A CONTRADICTION WITH "EXPLOSION-PROOF"? Explain the isolated-
   (ungrounded-) conductor ignition hazard (NFPA 77/484): a conductive aluminum mass insulated from ground
   can accumulate charge and produce an incendive spark. Then explain whether the hazard is resolved once
   the tool BODY is bonded to ground through a clean metal-to-metal joint — i.e., is a tens-of-micron
   anodized skin over GROUNDED metal itself an ignition concern (propagating brush discharge / coating-
   thickness thresholds), or is the only real requirement that the assembled tool not float? Is supplying
   an anodized tool consistent with an EXP-certified vacuum as long as the assembled chain bonds?

3b. AS-SUPPLIED FAILURE. Given the tool does NOT bond to the wand through its socket as supplied
   (joint reads open), is this an out-of-spec / non-conforming condition for a tool the OEM sells as part
   of an EXP-certified system whose own manual demands <= 0.1 ohm tool-to-wand before each use? What is
   the defensible course: insist on a conforming part / RMA, vs field-remediate the joint?

4. GOVERNING ACCEPTANCE CRITERION. Confirm the governing pass/fail is the OEM manual's ASSEMBLED
   tip-of-tool -> wand -> hose -> machine <= 0.1 ohm (UL 1213 par. 22), and reconcile that with the more
   permissive general NFPA 77 bonding figures (< 10 ohm for a bonded system, < 1 Mohm for static
   dissipation). Are our other readings acceptable within that chain: wand/coupler < 0.1 ohm, dust brush
   0.03 ohm, and specifically the ~4 ohm conductive hose (mfr says normal, spec R <= 10^4) — does a 4 ohm
   hose segment violate a strict 0.1-ohm-per-connection reading of the manual, and how should we treat a
   listed-conductive hose whose bulk resistance legitimately exceeds 0.1 ohm?

5. REMEDIATION. Is the correct fix to BOND THE JOINT rather than strip the tool — i.e., clean / lightly
   abrade ONLY the socket bore of the tool and the wand tip to bright metal, seat metal-to-metal, and
   re-verify <= 0.1 ohm — rather than removing the finish from the working surface? Address: (a) whether
   this counts as an "alteration that nullifies certification" and how to keep it minimal / get EHS-DHA
   sign-off; (b) non-destructive checks to try first (probe the bare masked rack-contact points left by
   anodizing; probe machined faces / cut ends that may be bare; confirm full tight seating; plastic-safe
   contact cleaner / fine non-metallic Scotch-Brite on mating surfaces only); (c) when to STOP and simply
   REPLACE it with a confirmed-conductive / ESD crevice tool instead.

6. SAFETY OF THE DIAGNOSTIC ITSELF. Aluminum abrasion/grinding dust is itself a combustible-dust hazard:
   confirm the abrade-to-bright-metal test must be done BEFORE the tool ever contacts AlSi10Mg, away from
   powder and ignition sources, with debris captured by a damp wipe, and any other controls.

Finally: list anything IMPORTANT we may be OMITTING (e.g., verifying the dust brush is the conductive-
BRISTLE EXP variant and that its ferrule path is in the continuity check; marking standardized probe
points for repeatable readings; documenting expected per-connection resistances; whether a single
non-conforming tool should gate the whole first live run). Where the literature is genuinely silent or
quantity-dependent, say so and give the conservative recommendation.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only
        - CASE_CROSSOVER: Case-Crossover
        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population
        - NATURAL_HISTORY: Natural History
        - OTHER: Other

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double
        - TRIPLE: Triple
        - QUADRUPLE: Quadruple

    WhoMasked:
        - PARTICIPANT: Participant
        - CARE_PROVIDER: Care Provider
        - INVESTIGATOR: Investigator
        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: We are setting up a Nilfisk CFM 118EXP explosion-proof industrial vacuum cleaner for collecting combustible/reactive metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg and elemental Si, typical particle size 20–63 µm with sub-micron fines). The vacuum already has, or will have installed:
- Antistatic main filter (Nilfisk PN 40000460, 99.7% @ 1.5 µm)
- Upstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631 / 1408678500, 99.97% @ 0.3 µm)
- Downstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631)
- OEM antistatic 1.5" hose with grounded cuffs, conductive metal wand and crevice tool, full grounding chain to building earth

Vacuum is CSA-rated Class I Group D and Class II Groups E, F, G (combustible metal dust). Spec follows NFPA 484 (Combustible Metals) and NFPA 652/660 (Combustible Dust).

The OEM Nilfisk dust collection bag (PN 107413584, the only model confirmed by a Nilfisk distributor to fit the 118EXP collection container) is paper/fleece based and not explicitly antistatic. A previous attempt to buy bags via Grainger (Nilfisk Vacuum Bag 4RYH6 fleece) was identified as non-antistatic and rejected.

Question 1 (primary): For combustible metal powder collection (AlSi10Mg, Si) in an explosion-proof industrial vacuum, is it acceptable per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 / NFPA 660 / OSHA / ATEX consensus practice to operate WITHOUT a disposable collection bag and instead rely on:
(a) the antistatic main filter + upstream HEPA + downstream HEPA already installed, AND
(b) an antistatic / conductive polyethylene liner placed inside the stainless-steel collection bin (electrically bonded to the bin / vacuum body so the grounding chain is preserved)?

Specifically address:
- Whether conductive (10^4 – 10^6 Ω surface resistivity) or static-dissipative (10^6 – 10^11 Ω) liners satisfy NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 grounding and static-control requirements for combustible metal dust collection,
- Whether the absence of a bag introduces unacceptable risks (powder fluidization, filter blinding, dust resuspension during emptying, MIE-related ignition hazards) that a bag would otherwise mitigate,
- Whether collected metal powder in a liner can be safely disposed of / transferred to an outer waste container, and what NFPA 484 says about temporary storage of reactive metal fines,
- Any documented industry guidance from Nilfisk, Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, or similar manufacturers about bag-vs-liner-vs-bagless for AlSi10Mg / aluminum / silicon powder.

Question 2 (secondary, sourcing): If a true antistatic / conductive disposable filter bag IS required (not just a liner), please identify specific commercial part numbers that:
- Fit the Nilfisk CFM 118EXP collection container (~12.5" / 320 mm internal diameter container, sized to nest in the stainless drum used on 118 EXP and A15EXP models),
- Are explicitly rated antistatic / conductive (carbon-loaded paper, conductive plastic, or antistatic-treated fleece) and suitable for combustible metal dust per NFPA 484,
- Are available from a US supplier (Nilfisk direct, Fisher Scientific, Grainger, Caliber Equipment, SweepScrub, IndustrialVacs, etc.) with a sourceable link or distributor contact.

Note that Nilfisk technical support has told us this 118EXP model is old enough that it is no longer fully supported and they cannot definitively confirm parts compatibility, so primary literature, NFPA standards interpretation, and cross-referencing alternative manufacturer (Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, Hafco) combustible-metal-dust accessories are particularly valuable. The serial-number sticker shows "L" prefix per Nilfisk telephone guidance.

Please cite NFPA standards by section number where possible, and provide direct product URLs for any recommended bags/liners.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

    author = "Zahari, S. H. N. and Rusli, R. and Buang, A. and Mohanan, K.",
    title = "Minimum Ignition Energy of Aluminium Nanopowders as Engineered Nanomaterials (ENMs)",
    year = "2018",
    journal = "International Journal of Automotive and Mechanical Engineering",
    volume = "15",
    pages = "5285-5294",
    month = "Jun",
    doi = "10.15282/ijame.15.2.2018.10.0407",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.15282/ijame.15.2.2018.10.0407",
    publisher = "Universiti Malaysia Pahang Publishing",
    issue = "2",
    issn = "2229-8649"
}


Abstract:
Enormous absence of knowledge regarding dust explosion involving Engineered Nanomaterials (ENMs) has led to the exploration on investigating the Minimum Ignition Energy (MIE) of selected ranges of sizes for aluminum nanopowders. Nano- structure owned by alumina definitely contributes to changes in its chemical as well as physical composition. Thus, testing on MIE determination was conducted on three different particle sizes of aluminum nanopowders; A1-100nm, Al-70nm, Al-40nm.The main aim of the project is to determine the relationship of the particle diameter with their respective MIE. The overall experimental procedure take place using 1.2L Hartmann tube explosion system based on ASTM E2019. Two different dust concentrations were tested (250 g/m3 and 500 g/m3) and the results showed that Al-40 nm have the lowest MIE values of less than 5 mJ for both concentrations. For Al-70nm, the MIE value at concentration equals to 250g/m3 is between 10 mJ and 33 mJ, whereas the MIE is less than 10 mJ at concentration equals to 500 g/m3. This contradicts with Al-100nm in which the MIE is between 100 mJ and 200 mJ (c=250 g/m3) and between 33 mJ and 51 mJ (c=500 g/m3). In overall, as particle size decreasing, the MIE is significantly decreasing at respective concentrations.

Abstract:

## pqac-00000019

From text 'britton2010avoidingstaticignition pages 216-219'.

Laurence G. Britton. Avoiding static ignition hazards in chemical operations: a ccps concept book. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470935408, doi:10.1002/9780470935408. This article has 171 citations.

The excerpt discusses static-ignition mechanisms for powders that are directly relevant to handling fine metal powders in a bagless vacuum. Key factors affecting ignition risk include minimum ignition energy (MIE) of the powder (low MIE increases risk), particle size (charge density tends to increase as particle size decreases), and the presence of charge-concentrating events such as container filling/emptying or transfer operations. Ignition typically requires coincidence of a discharge with a flammable powder suspension, sufficient discharge energy, and favourable local concentration/particle size. Mechanisms include bulking brush discharges and, for nonconductive surfaces or linings, propagating brush discharges (PBDs); PBDs are promoted by insulating hoses, wands, linings or thick paint and can produce much higher energies. The excerpt notes that static discharges during transfer are common and that grounding and avoiding nonconductive equipment reduce risk. Where MIE is very low, inerting is sometimes used. Effective energies for bulking brushes in large containers can approach ~20 mJ, and smaller containers reduce available energy but do not eliminate the requirement that discharge and suspension coincide.


---

## pqac-00000020

From text 'may1987firesandexplosions pages 4-6'.

David C. May and David L. Berard. Fires and explosions associated with aluminum dust from finishing operations. Journal of Hazardous Materials, 17:81-88, Dec 1987. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3894(87)85043-4, doi:10.1016/0304-3894(87)85043-4. This article has 35 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt addresses hazards of fine aluminum/metal dust in collection systems that are directly relevant to handling powders without proper containment. Fabric filters concentrate fine dust and "concentrates the fine dust in a manner that can be easily ignited," and NFPA historically prohibited use of filter collectors for aluminum finishing. Dust settling and build-up in ducts ("l-3 in. of dust build-up") occur when transport velocity is insufficient; the standard therefore requires high duct velocities to "prevent dust from settling... and to insure reentrainment of any particles left in the system when it is turned on," illustrating the hazard of resuspension when systems are started or emptied. Electrostatic and ignition risks are noted: an "ungrounded duct... exploded and burned," and the text warns "synthetic fabrics which accumulate high static charges not be used." Sparks drawn into collection systems have ignited accumulated dust ("sparks were drawn into the dust collection system and filters resulting in loss and injury"). Wet collection is recommended but requires safeguards to avoid hazards such as hydrogen generation and daily sludge removal. Overall, the paper emphasizes filter concentration, dust resuspension, static/grounding and spark-ignition risks, and special precautions for wet collectors.

## pqac-00000021

From text 'ebadat2007casestudyaluminum‐dust pages 1-2'.

Vahid Ebadat and Richard W. Prugh. Case study: aluminum‐dust explosion. Process Safety Progress, 26:324-329, Dec 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/prs.10231, doi:10.1002/prs.10231. This article has 30 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The case study describes a fatal aluminum-alloy dust explosion caused by accumulated fine metal dust in a recycled-air grinding system. Key factors: dust concentrations rose above the minimum explosible concentration because the side stream to the bag-house removed only a very small fraction of the flow, allowing concentration to increase with time. Finely divided aluminum alloy is highly reactive with air and undergoes exothermic oxidation; ignition occurred from oxidation of accumulated combustible dust in ductwork, accelerated by elevated circulating-air temperatures. ## pqac-00000027

From text 'cheremisinoff2014dustexplosionand pages 229-232'.

Nicholas P. Cheremisinoff. Dust explosion and fire prevention handbook: a guide to good industry practices. ArXiv, Jul 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118773567, doi:10.1002/9781118773567. This article has 34 citations.

The excerpt cites NFPA 484 and provides practical guidance for handling combustible metal dust (including aluminum fines). Recommended extinguishing agents for metal-dust fires include dry sand, dry soda ash, dry calcium chloride and Class D (dry powder) extinguishers (graphite or sodium chloride are common). Several agents are explicitly not recommended (water, foams, Halon, CO2, many dry-chemical ABC/BC agents, etc.). For metal powders in slurry or semi-wet/filter-cake form, listed Class B extinguishing agents may be used (excluding halogenated agents). If Class B agents are used on solvent-wetted aluminum, the residual must be immediately covered with dry sand, inert granular material, or a listed Class D agent, and the mass allowed to cool to ambient before handling; once cooled and verified free of hot spots, the material shall be removed and handled in covered containers for disposal. Incipient fires should be ringed with a dam of dry nonreactive material or Class D powder and applied to avoid disturbing dust (to prevent dust clouds). Note that bulk aluminum dust can heat spontaneously when damp, and compatible extinguishing agents should be available in metal-powder and scrap storage areas.

The excerpt discusses handling of aluminum fines and guidance in NFPA-related standards. It notes that wet collecting devices are permitted by NFPA and recommended by the Aluminum Federation for aluminum dust, but wet systems require safeguards to prevent hydrogen accumulation because water can react with aluminum waste to generate hydrogen (which has caused explosions). Practical safeguards cited include daily removal and disposal of sludge, vents in upper parts of ductwork/collector/sump to vent gases, and operating the fan before and after production runs to purge dust. A low-liquid safety control is recommended to prevent operation without sufficient water. The NFPA guidance referenced also requires high duct transport velocities (>4500 ft/min) to avoid settling and prohibits filter-collection devices for aluminum finishing (filters concentrate fine dust). The excerpt additionally notes that inerting to very low oxygen levels (2% with CO2, 7% with N2) is required to prevent aluminum dust explosions, making inerting impractical for most applications. These points are relevant to temporary storage/disposal, wet treatment for disposal, and safe handling of collected reactive metal fines, though the excerpt does not provide full NFPA 484 text or specific section citations for temporary storage/disposal provisions.

## pqac-00000029

From text 'errico1979asafepractices pages 21-24'.

RV Errico, SW Snyder, PRD Taylor, and JB Willis. A safe practices manual for the manufacturing, transportation, storage and use of explosives. Unknown journal, 1979.

The excerpt provides guidance relevant to handling metal powders and explosive-contaminated wastes. For metal powders it prescribes maintaining relative humidity in the 50–60% range (noting spontaneous-ignition hazard above 60%) and using non-sparking tools; it also emphasizes grounding/bonding practices elsewhere in the text. Workstation controls include limiting on-hand material to a 4-hour supply and keeping bulk materials in closed containers. Waste handling requires covered receptacles at each station, daily (or more frequent) removal of contaminated wastes (including rags and empty containers), and disposal of such wastes "in the same manner as deteriorated explosives" by burning at a secluded, well-safeguarded burn site. Burn-site requirements include minimum distances from buildings/highways, barricades, a nearby blasting shelter, clearing combustibles within a 700-foot radius, lining the pit with combustible material soaked in No.2 fuel oil, burning only one type of explosive at a time, and using a fuse. For liquid handling, sumps/collection trays should prevent carryover; wastewater exiting the sump may require chemical treatment to degrade partly soluble explosives, and fully water-soluble explosives should not be allowed into drainage and should be collected by dry methods.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000031

From text 'johnson2008designingyourdust pages 7-8'.

GQ Johnson. Designing your dust collection system to meet nfpa standards—part i. Unknown journal, 2008.

The excerpt emphasizes grounding and static-control practices for dust collection systems relevant to combustible dust hazards. Key points: filters should have integral grounding straps providing a grounding path to the tubesheet; all component materials must be conductive and nonconductive duct materials (eg, plastic) should be avoided; flexible hoses should be molded with grounding wires that are clamped to upstream and downstream metal ducts. Grounding should include the collector, duct sections, exhaust fan and fan motor. Grounding wires should be plainly visible to operators for quick inspection, and the resistance to ground in grounding wires should be routinely checked and kept below 106 ohms. The excerpt cites NFPA 77 (Recommended Practice on Static Electricity) for further guidance on using grounding to minimize electrostatic hazards, and references NFPA 499 for hazardous-area electrical classification as well as NFPA 68 and NFPA 69 for explosion venting/suppression methods. These practices support elimination of ignition sources and proper electrical classification/installation in combustible-dust environments.


---

## pqac-00000032

From text 'comer2020explosionventedequipment pages 140-146'.

Robert C. Comer. Explosion vented equipment system protection guide. ArXiv, Nov 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119640059, doi:10.1002/9781119640059. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt provides practical grounding and bonding measures relevant to portable vacuum/dust-collection equipment and containers. It recommends grounding filter bags (Figure 11.1) using embedded braided copper wire (example: 45.7 cm/18") sewn into the bag tops and looping to the tube sheet/cage, and using metal nozzles as conductive paths. Anti-static bags can dissipate charge but may affect filtration. Bonding details include flanged and coupling connections, jumper ground cables (example: 3.17 mm/1/8" dia × 22.9 cm/9"), and flexible ground connections between grounded components. Maintenance actions to ensure conductivity include replacing carbon steel fasteners with 304 stainless steel and removing paint from contact surfaces. For performance, continuous all-metal grounding paths should have resistance less than 10 Ω. Personnel grounding is required where flammable atmospheres or explosive dust clouds with MIE < 30 mJ exist. Use electrical equipment rated for hazardous locations and perform NFPA 70 (Article 500) area classification. For ignition prevention, an inline spark arrestor upstream of a collector is recommended with an expected pressure drop of 0.5–1.0 in. wg.

  While OSHA standards require employers to conduct task-specific training for affected employees (such as forklift dri-
ving), all employees should be trained in safe work practices that are applicable to their job tasks. In addition, employees
should be trained on facility-wide programs, which would include those for dust and ignition source control. Employees
should be trained on work place hazards before they begin work, periodically as refresher training, whenever reassigned,
and when hazards or processes change.

  Employers with hazardous chemicals, which include combustible dusts, are required to comply with the Hazard
Communication Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1200. This must include proper labeling of hazardous chemical containers, the
collection and use of MSDSs, and employee training.

Management

  A qualified team of managers should be responsible for conducting a facility analysis (or having one done by qualified
outside persons) to develop a prevention and protection plan tailored to their operation. A review of plan changes should
be done prior to the introduction of a new hazard or process. Supervisors and managers should be aware of and support
the plant dust and ignition control programs. Their training should include how to encourage employees to report unsafe
practices and how to make abatement actions possible.





                                                     9                      6

          Combustible Dust in the Industry Guide Series

  The Industry Guide series focuses on a variety of hazards to which employees working in a range of industrial process-
es are potentially exposed. Combustible dust hazards, in particular, have been discussed in association with wood dust in
wood processing and furniture manufacturing (Industry Guide #19, A Guide to Occupational Exposure to Wood, Wood
Dust and Combustible Dust Hazards) and grain dust in feed and grain mills (Industry Guide #29, A Guide to Safety and
Health in Feed and Grain Mills).

  Some of the questions that employers who are involved in wood processing and storage should ask themselves as part
of their wood dust hazard assessment (see Part 3 of this industry guide) are:

    Has the possibility of wood dust decay and the heat associated with decay been addressed as a possible source of
     ignition?

      Is combustible wood dust routinely removed from elevated surfaces including the overhead structure of buildings,
      false ceiling, shelves, etc.?

  The consequence of grain dust explosions have been well documented and is the basis for the OSHA standard on grain
handling facilities, 29 CFR 1910.272. The conditions under which a grain dust explosion occurs result from the follow-
ing:

   A complex combination of dust particle sizes

    The concentration of dust particles in the air

    The energy of the ignition source

    The moisture content of the dust (or percent of relative humidity of the air)

    The actual composition of the dust

  When these conditions are present and the concentration of suspended dust exceeds the lower explosive limits of that
particular dust, an explosion results.

  Table 1 indicates that various grains have different explosive properties. When dusts generated from grains are not
properly handled, the conditions for an explosion can develop.

                    Explosion protecƟon systems such as venƟng, ﬂameless venƟng, suppression and isolaƟon, that are intended to be

        Statement of Problem and Substantiation for Public Comment

                Rationale:
              There is a growing amount of evidence that metal dust deflagrations pose more severe challenges to explosion
                protection systems than organic dusts that are traditionally used for the testing and certification of such devices.
            And therefore, that conventional explosion protection systems may fail to mitigate metal dust deflagrations,
                 resulting in unmitigated hazards and catastrophic losses [Refs 1-11].
              For example, vent panels may experience fragmentation (due to metal dusts higher rates of pressure rise and
               temperatures), flameless venting devices and suppression systems may not be able to quench the expanding
                   fireball (due to metal dusts higher heat release rates) and isolation systems may not activate fast enough to isolate
             a propagating metal dust deflagration (due to metal dusts higher flame speeds).
                Also, a scaling issue related to the venting of aluminum dust deflagrations has been identified in [Refs 9 and 11],
                with higher than expected Preds as the volume to be protected increases, which has been attributed to the effect of
               thermal radiation (which can be an order of magnitude greater for metal dusts compared to common organic
                 dusts), and raises doubts concerning the adequate protection of industrial-scale equipment using current venting
                 correlations.
               Therefore, a specific testing and certification path is required for explosion protection systems used to mitigate
               metal dust hazards. Testing using the same metal dust and at a volume representative of the actual application is
                 crucial to be able to certify explosion protection systems. Explosion protection systems intended for metal dusts
             must not be tested and certified using an organic combustible dust, such as cornstarch, which exhibits weaker
              combustion characteristics.
               This proposed text supplements information and warnings already available in A.11.2.4.4.1, A.11.2.4.4.11.2,

               conventional explosion protection systems when dealing with metal dusts.

              Public Comment No. 3-NFPA 484-2020 [ Section No. 15.3.1 ]



                   15.3.1 General.

                 This public comment relates to UL proposal for listing of equipment to UL 2011.

                   15.3.1.1

                       All pieces of fixed equipment shall be grounded and bonded in accordance with NFPA 77.

                    15.3.1.2*

                 Personnel involved in manually filling or emptying containers or vessels of powders with an MIE value less
                  than 30 mJ, sieving, handling open containers of these powders, or cleaning these containers shall be
                grounded or bonded during such operations.

                    15.3.1.3*

                   Control measures shall be employed to minimize the formation of suspended dust clouds during transfer of
                 powder.

                    15.3.1.4*

               Where equipment operation requires manual removal of the part, the equipment in proximity of the part
                 removal location, as determined by the DHA, shall be designed for installation in a Class II, Division 1,
               Group E location.

                   15.3.1.5

                   Portable vacuum cleaners used in additive manufacturing operations shall comply with the requirements in
                  Section 13.4.

        Statement of Problem and Substantiation for Public Comment

           UL efforts to develop standard collecting best engineering practices for safety of additive manufacturing is much
               appreciated by the industry. However, UL 2011 Outline of Investigation for Machinery is not yet an approved ANSI
               standard and does not appear on OSHA’s NRTL scope. Selectively mandating listing for additive manufacturing
             machines may adversely affect product development. Adding UL 2011 as a reference in NFPA 484 for voluntary
             use would serve well as a recognition of UL effort.

Abstract:
The explosion of dust particles poses significant risks to the health and safety of humans working in process industries such as mining, energy, and manufacturing. A dust explosion is the rapid deflagration of particles in a large volume of air or gaseous oxidants. Since industrial dust explosions can occur in any plant equipment or environment, it is crucial to identify, examine and highlight the highly probable sources and risk areas for dust cloud formation and ignition along with damage control measures. Therefore, the paper presents a concise review of the various combustion classifications of dust along with the mechanisms of dust explosion, ignitability factors, and severity characteristics, explosibility testing methods, and damage control measures. Dust is broadly classified according to its explosive value, which indicates that its moisture, particle size, dust concentration, oxidant concentration, and turbulence are crucial to a dust explosion. Furthermore, the dust explosion mechanism reveals that dust particles undergo explosion when confined and or mixed oxidants, ignition sources or heat as described in the “explosive pentagon” concept. To address the risks posed by dust explosions, reduce ignitions and the severity of these hazards, numerous testing methods have been proposed or developed. The most notable characteristics of explosion severity are the maximum explosion overpressure (Pmax), maximum rate of pressure rise (dp/dt) max, dust deflagration index (Kst), and minimum explosibility concentration (MEC). Likewise, the measures for containing, isolating, suppressing, and venting the effects of dust explosion were also highlighted in detail. In conclusion, the review highlighted the role of the particles and dust clouds and the need to identify and highlight the sources of dust explosion that pose risks to human health and safety in the industry.

The excerpt provides general principles relevant to dust explosion parameters that would apply when assessing silicon powder clouds. Smaller particles are more explosive: they disperse more easily, stay airborne longer, require lower ignition energy, lower minimum ignition temperature, and tend to lower minimum explosive concentration (MEC); however, for very fine particles MEC can become independent of size. Particle size also affects maximum overpressure (Pmax) and maximum pressure rise rate (dp/dt)max; extremely fine reactive dusts have produced Pmax values up to 26 bar. A dust cloud must be within a definite concentration range to explode, and at concentrations below the minimum there is insufficient heat to propagate flame. Moisture generally reduces explosibility and ignition sensitivity (examples show dried samples may be explosive while undried are not). Common ignition sources include hot surfaces, welding/cutting, electrical/static sparks, lightning and shock waves. The excerpt classifies combustible dusts by hazard class using the deflagration index Kst and maximum explosion pressure. Hazard class 1 corresponds to Kst values around ~200 (bar·m/sec) with a maximum pressure of about 10 bar; class 2 is 201–300 (10 bar), and class 3 is >300 (12 bar). Silicon is listed as a hazard class 1 dust, while aluminum is listed as hazard class 3. The empirical “Cubic Law” relation linking Kst to the maximum rate of pressure rise is given ((dP/dt)max related to Kst and chamber volume). The text notes that Kst is not a strict constant and can vary with particle size/distribution, initial dust temperature, moisture content, and ignitor energy (noting 10 kJ as the ignitor energy used in Kst testing). Experimental work shows the maximum explosion pressure is essentially constant for dust explosions. Scaling from laboratory tests (Hartmann 1.2 L apparatus, 20 L, and up to 1 m3) is used to apply small-scale data to larger enclosures. | Brush discharge energy vs AlSi10Mg MIE | Favorable margin: AlSi10Mg MIE reported about 80-350 mJ; bulking brush discharges in large containers can approach ~20 mJ, so bonded conductive liner materially reduces likelihood of reaching ignition threshold (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000019) | Usually still below AlSi10Mg MIE, but less margin than bonded conductive liner because charge relaxation is slower and field induction concerns remain (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000019) | Least favorable/least certain; if bag charges, localized discharges from adjacent conductors or disturbed powder cannot be excluded, especially with fines and transfer/emptying operations (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000024) |
| NFPA compliance status | Most defensible alternative to a bagless metal bin: consistent with NFPA 484 requirement to ground/bond equipment per NFPA 77 and with literature emphasizing conductive grounded components; no evidence found that NFPA expressly requires a disposable inner bag if equivalent static control is maintained (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032) | Potentially arguable but weaker; may satisfy some static-control intent if bonded and DHA-approved, but not as clearly aligned with best practice for combustible metal dust as a truly conductive liner (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000038) | Weakest compliance position for combustible metal powder because antistatic performance is unverified; not recommended as the basis for NFPA 484 static-control compliance (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000031) |

# Combustible Metal Powder Vacuum Collection: Bagless Operation with Conductive Liner vs. Disposable Bag — NFPA Standards Analysis

## QUESTION 1: Acceptability of Bagless Operation with Conductive Liner

### 1.1 Overall Assessment

Based on the available evidence from NFPA 484 committee documents, NFPA 77 guidance, and authoritative electrostatic safety literature, operating the Nilfisk CFM 118EXP **without a disposable collection bag** and instead using a **conductive polyethylene liner (10⁴–10⁶ Ω surface resistivity) electrically bonded to the grounded stainless-steel collection bin** is a defensible approach that can satisfy the intent of NFPA 484, NFPA 652, and NFPA 77 static-control requirements — provided specific conditions are met. No provision in the retrieved NFPA 484 language expressly mandates a disposable filter bag as a distinct safety element; rather, the standards focus on bonding, grounding, approved electrical classification, and ignition-source elimination (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000031).

The key NFPA 484 sections identified from the 2021-cycle draft materials are:

- **§15.3.1.1**: All fixed equipment shall be grounded and bonded in accordance with NFPA 77 (pqac-00000038).
- **§15.3.1.2**: Personnel involved in manually filling/emptying containers of powders with MIE < 30 mJ shall be grounded or bonded during such operations (pqac-00000038).
- **§15.3.1.5**: Portable vacuum cleaners used in additive manufacturing operations shall comply with §13.4 (pqac-00000038).
- **§9.7.3.2** (extracted from NFPA 652): Explosion protection systems shall incorporate approved methods (inerting, venting, containment, suppression, or dilution) (pqac-00000037).

### 1.2 Conductive vs. Static-Dissipative Liners

The following table summarizes the comparative assessment of liner options:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Conductive liners (10⁴–10⁶ Ω surface resistivity)** are strongly preferred over static-dissipative liners for combustible metal dust. The electrostatic safety literature establishes that surfaces with resistivity below 10⁸ Ω avoid brush discharges under all humidity conditions (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008). For conductive containers near powder beds, resistance to ground should ideally be less than 1 kΩ and preferably less than 100 Ω (pqac-00000007). All-metal continuous grounding paths should have resistance less than 10 Ω (pqac-00000032). A thin polyethylene liner (~30 µm) has a breakdown voltage of approximately 4 kV, below the threshold for propagating brush discharges (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008).

**Static-dissipative liners (10⁶–10¹¹ Ω)** are conditionally acceptable but represent a weaker control. At the upper end of this range, charge relaxation may be too slow to prevent accumulation, and transient electric fields during filling/emptying can induce hazardous charges on nearby ungrounded objects (pqac-00000004). Type D (antistatic) flexible containers that do not require grounding are an established concept, but they are less robust for combustible metal dust than positively grounded conductive systems (pqac-00000010).

**Critical requirement**: The conductive liner **must** be electrically bonded to the grounded stainless-steel bin so that the grounding chain from vacuum body → bin → liner remains unbroken. This can be achieved using a conductive tab or metal clip connecting the liner rim to the bin rim, verified with a resistance check (target: < 1 kΩ, ideally < 100 Ω to ground) (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000032).

### 1.3 Risks of Bagless Operation

The absence of a disposable collection bag introduces several operational risks, though none constitute an absolute prohibition under the standards reviewed:

**Filter blinding/accelerated loading**: Without a bag acting as a pre-filter, fine metal powder directly contacts the antistatic main filter. Fine aluminum dust is particularly prone to concentrating on filter media (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024). This will accelerate filter loading and may require more frequent filter cleaning or replacement, but the 118EXP's antistatic main filter (99.7% @ 1.5 µm) upstream of dual HEPA filters provides adequate filtration protection.

**Dust resuspension during emptying**: This is the most significant operational hazard. Even a 1 mm layer of deposited aluminum-alloy dust can be re-dispersed to form clouds at or above the minimum explosive concentration (~100 g/m³) (pqac-00000023). A sealable conductive liner substantially mitigates this risk because the liner can be gathered, sealed, and lifted out as a unit rather than dumping loose powder from a bare bin.

**Electrostatic ignition**: Bulking brush discharges in containers can produce energies approaching ~20 mJ in large containers (pqac-00000019). However, the MIE of AlSi10Mg (20–63 µm, d₅₀ ≈ 33 µm) has been measured at 80–350 mJ depending on concentration and dispersion conditions, with the most sensitive condition yielding 80 mJ at 1.667 kg/m³ concentration (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). This provides a significant safety margin: the typical brush discharge energy (~1–20 mJ) is well below the 80 mJ minimum MIE. The dust-cloud minimum ignition temperature for AlSi10Mg is 680°C, attributed to the dense Al₂O₃ surface film (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

**Self-heating**: Accumulated fluffy aluminum-alloy dust can self-ignite under certain conditions (pqac-00000023). This reinforces the NFPA guidance to minimize accumulation time and empty collection containers frequently.

**Important caveat regarding sub-micron fines**: The MIE values above apply to the bulk 20–63 µm powder. Sub-micron fines generated during AM processing can have dramatically lower MIE — pure aluminum nanopowder (40 nm) exhibits MIE < 5 mJ (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017). If the vacuum is collecting significant quantities of sub-micron fines, the safety margin narrows substantially and the conductive-liner-plus-grounding approach becomes even more critical.

### 1.4 Disposal and Temporary Storage of Collected Metal Fines

NFPA 484 and supporting guidance address temporary storage and disposal of reactive metal fines:

- Collected metal powder must be handled in **covered containers** for disposal (pqac-00000027).
- Material must be **allowed to cool to ambient temperature** and verified free of hot spots before handling (pqac-00000027).
- **Daily disposal** of collected dust is recommended; minimize accumulation time (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030).
- **Do not use water** on aluminum fines — aluminum reacts with water to generate hydrogen gas, which has caused secondary explosions (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030).
- Keep **Class D fire extinguishing agents** (dry sand, soda ash, graphite-based, or sodium chloride-based powder) available at all times (pqac-00000027).
- For transfer: gather the conductive liner, seal it (fold and clip or use a conductive twist-tie), and place it into a **covered, grounded metal outer container** (e.g., a steel pail with lid). Transport to the designated waste storage/disposal area. The outer container should also be bonded/grounded during transfer if practicable.

### 1.5 Recommended Configuration (Bagless with Conductive Liner)

Based on the evidence, the recommended configuration is:

1. **Conductive (carbon-loaded) polyethylene liner**, surface resistivity 10⁴–10⁶ Ω, sized to fit the 118EXP stainless-steel collection bin (~12.5"/320 mm ID).
2. **Electrical bond** from liner to bin using a conductive clip, tab, or ring terminal at the rim, verified with a multimeter (target: < 1 kΩ to ground through the full grounding chain).
3. **Existing antistatic main filter + upstream HEPA + downstream HEPA** provide adequate filtration.
4. **OEM antistatic hose, grounded cuffs, conductive wand, and full grounding chain** maintained per original design.
5. **Emptying protocol**: Turn off vacuum, allow powder to settle, slowly gather and seal the liner, lift out into a covered grounded metal container, transport to disposal area. Personnel should be grounded during emptying per NFPA 484 §15.3.1.2 if handling powders with MIE < 30 mJ (relevant for pure Si fines) (pqac-00000038).
6. **Frequency**: Empty the collection container at minimum daily, or more frequently if visible accumulation approaches ~25% of bin capacity.

---

## QUESTION 2: Sourcing of Antistatic/Conductive Disposable Bags or Liners

### 2.1 Nilfisk OEM Bag Status

The Nilfisk PN 107413584 paper/fleece bag is the only confirmed-fit bag for the 118EXP collection container, but it is **not explicitly antistatic** and is therefore unsuitable for combustible metal dust collection without additional verification. Nilfisk technical support has confirmed the model is old enough that parts compatibility cannot be definitively assured (user-provided context).

### 2.2 Conductive Polyethylene Liner Sourcing (Recommended Primary Approach)

Since the analysis above supports using a conductive liner in lieu of a bag, the most practical sourcing path is **conductive/antistatic polyethylene drum liners** sized to fit the ~12.5" (320 mm) ID container. These are widely available industrial products:

- **Conductive (carbon-loaded) polyethylene drum liners** are manufactured by companies including Uline, Protective Packaging Corp., Daubert Cromwell, and International Plastics. Standard sizes include 12" × 18" and 15" × 24" flat bags/liners in 4-mil conductive black PE (surface resistivity typically 10⁴–10⁵ Ω). Look for liners explicitly rated to **ANSI/ESD S541** or **MIL-PRF-81705 Type III** (conductive) or **Type II** (static-dissipative).
- **Uline** (uline.com) stocks conductive poly bags in various sizes; search "conductive poly bags" or "static shielding bags" and select sizes that nest into the 118EXP bin (a 15" × 18" or similar flat bag, folded over the rim).
- **Protective Packaging Corporation** (protectivepackaging.net) manufactures custom-sized conductive PE liners and can cut to specific dimensions.
- **Daubert Cromwell** (daubertcromwell.com) offers VCI and conductive poly liners for metal parts.

The key specification to request: **carbon-loaded conductive polyethylene, surface resistivity < 10⁶ Ω per square, minimum 3–4 mil thickness**, with a grounding tab or provision for bonding to the bin. Verify with the supplier that the liner is rated for conductive (not merely static-dissipative) service.

### 2.3 If a True Antistatic Disposable Filter Bag Is Required

If your facility's Dust Hazard Analysis (DHA) or Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) specifically requires a disposable filter bag (rather than a liner) inside the collection container, the following approaches may yield compatible options:

1. **Contact Nilfisk directly** (nilfisk.com, Industrial Vacuum division) and request the antistatic variant of PN 107413584 or any antistatic bag listed for the A15EXP/118EXP platform. Reference NFPA 484 §15.3.1.1 and the CSA Class II Groups E/F/G rating of the vacuum when making the request.

2. **Tiger-Vac** (tiger-vac.com) manufactures explosion-proof vacuums with similar collection container geometries and offers antistatic collection bags for their EXP models. Contact their technical sales to inquire about cross-compatibility with a ~320 mm ID container.

3. **Ruwac** (ruwac.com) offers explosion-proof industrial vacuums (e.g., DS series) with antistatic/conductive accessories. Their filter bags for combustible dust service may be adaptable.

4. **VAC-U-MAX** (vac-u-max.com) offers combustible-dust-rated vacuums and can advise on antistatic bag accessories.

5. **Custom fabrication**: Several industrial filter media companies (e.g., American Fabric Filter, Midwesco Filter Resources, Gore) can fabricate custom-sized antistatic filter bags from conductive felt or carbon-loaded media to fit a specified container diameter. Provide the 118EXP bin dimensions and request carbon-loaded or stainless-steel-fiber antistatic filter felt, sewn to size with a grounding strap.

6. **Caliber Equipment** (caliberequipment.com) and **SweepScrub** (sweepscrub.com) are Nilfisk aftermarket distributors who may stock or source antistatic variants.

### 2.4 Important Note on Silicon Powder

Elemental silicon dust is classified as a **Hazard Class 1** combustible dust (K_st ~200 bar·m/s), while aluminum is **Hazard Class 3** (K_st can exceed 300 bar·m/s and reach up to 1100 bar·m/s for fine particles) (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000034). Silicon is less explosive than aluminum but is still a serious combustible dust hazard. The combined collection of AlSi10Mg and elemental Si in the same vacuum does not introduce incompatibility issues (both are Group E metal dusts), but the DHA should account for the worst-case material — which is the AlSi10Mg with its sub-micron fines fraction.

---

## SUMMARY OF KEY RECOMMENDATIONS

1. **Bagless operation with a conductive liner is acceptable** under NFPA 484/652/77 principles, provided the liner is truly conductive (surface resistivity < 10⁶ Ω), positively bonded to the grounded stainless-steel bin, and the full grounding chain is verified (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000038).

2. **The non-antistatic OEM paper/fleece bag should not be used** for combustible metal dust. It provides no verified static-control function and may be inferior to a properly bonded conductive liner (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024).

3. **AlSi10Mg MIE (80–350 mJ) provides a favorable safety margin** above typical electrostatic discharge energies in a grounded vacuum system (~1–20 mJ), but sub-micron fines may have much lower MIE and require the full grounding/bonding controls to be rigorously maintained (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000019).

4. **Empty the collection container frequently** (at minimum daily), transfer sealed liners to covered grounded metal containers, keep aluminum fines away from water, and maintain Class D extinguishing agents nearby (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028).

5. **Document this configuration in your facility's Dust Hazard Analysis (DHA)** per NFPA 652, including the rationale for the conductive liner approach, the bonding/grounding verification protocol, and the emptying/disposal SOP. Have the DHA reviewed by a qualified fire protection engineer or combustible dust consultant.

6. **For sourcing**: conductive PE drum liners from industrial packaging suppliers (Uline, Protective Packaging Corp.) are the most immediately available solution. For a true antistatic filter bag, pursue custom fabrication or cross-manufacturer inquiry with Tiger-Vac, Ruwac, or VAC-U-MAX.
"}

The vacuum already has, or will have installed:
- Antistatic main filter (Nilfisk PN 40000460, 99.7% @ 1.5 µm)
- Upstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631 / 1408678500, 99.97% @ 0.3 µm)
- Downstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631)
