contexts.context: The excerpt discusses static-ignition mechanisms for powders that are directly relevant to handling fine metal powders in a bagless vacuum. Key factors affecting ignition risk include minimum ignition energy (MIE) of the powder (low MIE increases risk), particle size (charge density tends to increase as particle size decreases), and the presence of charge-concentrating events such as container filling/emptying or transfer operations. Ignition typically requires coincidence of a discharge with a flammable powder suspension, sufficient discharge energy, and favourable local concentration/particle size. Mechanisms include bulking brush discharges and, for nonconductive surfaces or linings, propagating brush discharges (PBDs); PBDs are promoted by insulating hoses, wands, linings or thick paint and can produce much higher energies. The excerpt notes that static discharges during transfer are common and that grounding and avoiding nonconductive equipment reduce risk. Where MIE is very low, inerting is sometimes used. Effective energies for bulking brushes in large containers can approach ~20 mJ, and smaller containers reduce available energy but do not eliminate the requirement that discharge and suspension coincide.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses static-ignition mechanisms relevant to handling fine powders. It notes that dust can be ignited by transitional or bulking brush discharges from nonconductive surfaces (for example plastic-coated metal), and that sparks may occur where conductive powder contacts a nonconductive container or lining. Conductive objects introduced into or near charged powder beds (e.g., bag-house components or probes) can be struck by brush discharges, producing sparks that ignite accumulated and suspended fine dust. Charge transfers from bulking brushes can be on the order of 10 µC; experiments showed that collected brush charge (>280 nC) routed through a spark gap ignited very sensitive dust (sulfur, MIE ≈ 1 mJ). To prevent indirect sparking, conductive objects need low resistance to ground (preferably <100 Ω, certainly <1 kΩ) to keep potentials below ~1 kV. The text also warns that broken conductive elements in hoses can form internal/external spark gaps and that plastic components (venturis, isolating linings) that isolate conductive parts increase ignition risk.

It notes that vacuuming is commonly used to empty bulk powder containers and specifically recommends conductive vacuum hoses to avoid ignition of flammable powders and nuisance shocks, because non-conductive hoses can produce incendive discharges from the fabric. contexts.context: The case study describes a fatal aluminum-alloy dust explosion caused by accumulated fine metal dust in a recycled-air grinding system. Key factors: dust concentrations rose above the minimum explosible concentration because the side stream to the bag-house removed only a very small fraction of the flow, allowing concentration to increase with time. Finely divided aluminum alloy is highly reactive with air and undergoes exothermic oxidation; ignition occurred from oxidation of accumulated combustible dust in ductwork, accelerated by elevated circulating-air temperatures. The system lacked inerting, heat removal, explosion venting, and procedures for emptying the dust collector; the cyclone became too hot to touch and the dust collector was inside the operating area. An access door was forcibly ejected and the resulting dust fireball ignited nearby LPG vapors. These observations support risks you listed: filter/blinding and high dust loading leading to explosive dust/air mixtures, heat buildup and self-heating of accumulated dust, hazards from emptying or disturbing accumulated dust, and potential for a dust fire to ignite nearby flammable sources. The report underscores that accumulated fine metal powder in metal housings or collectors can oxidize and ignite if not properly controlled.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents how handling and cleaning of metal dust collectors can create severe explosion risks. Even very thin deposited dust layers can be re-dispersed to form clouds at or above minimum explosive concentrations (example: a 1-mm layer can yield ~100 g/m3). Manual disturbance or inadequate filtration/cleaning (manual shaking replacing automated bag cleaning) allowed filter dust to be dislodged and contact a self-heating ignition source in the collection barrel; the dust collected on filter bags was shaken off and ignited by burning dust below. The authors conclude self-ignition of fluffy aluminium-alloy dust in the collector was the primary ignition source, and that accumulated deposited dust greatly increased propagation and consequences. They also note unusual combustion behavior ("combustion of aluminium steam") and warn that invisibility of airborne dust is not a reliable indicator of safety. Applied to a vacuum cleaner without a collection bag: risks include re-dispersion of settled fine metal powder into explosive concentrations, ignition in the collection vessel via self-heating or hot particles, increased propagation if dust accumulates, and elevated hazard when manual disturbance or poor filtration occurs.

Small particles are particularly hazardous because equipment can concentrate them: "They inherently concentrate the smaller particles, which are easier to ignite..." contexts.context: The excerpt notes that NFPA 484 (2015) contains detailed guidance and safety recommendations for dust collecting systems in facilities handling metal dusts. Wet-type abatement systems are generally preferred over dry collectors because they are inherently safer, but wet systems still require careful monitoring and maintenance (e.g., a lowered scrubber water level reduced abatement efficiency, reduced conveying velocity, allowed powder to settle, and possibly overheat and explode). Dry collectors must meet similar operational controls; loose parts in dry systems have acted as ignition sources in case studies. A minimum conveying velocity is recommended to prevent powder accumulation. NFPA 484 specifically prohibits recycling exhaust air from dry-type dust collectors back into buildings, since this can cause hazardous secondary explosions. The authors also emphasize that explosion isolation systems in ducting could have substantially limited deflagration consequences. Finally, aluminum dust exhibits very high flame temperatures, explosion pressures, KSt values and heat of combustion, indicating greater hazard than typical carbonaceous dusts—supporting the need for stringent storage, handling, and disposal controls.

Key lessons: static discharge is a common ignition source for fine metal dusts (notably aluminum), and PVC piping and similar systems can generate static; bonding and grounding of dust transport systems is recommended. contexts.context: The excerpt cites NFPA 484 and provides practical guidance for handling combustible metal dust (including aluminum fines). Recommended extinguishing agents for metal-dust fires include dry sand, dry soda ash, dry calcium chloride and Class D (dry powder) extinguishers (graphite or sodium chloride are common). Several agents are explicitly not recommended (water, foams, Halon, CO2, many dry-chemical ABC/BC agents, etc.). For metal powders in slurry or semi-wet/filter-cake form, listed Class B extinguishing agents may be used (excluding halogenated agents). If Class B agents are used on solvent-wetted aluminum, the residual must be immediately covered with dry sand, inert granular material, or a listed Class D agent, and the mass allowed to cool to ambient before handling; once cooled and verified free of hot spots, the material shall be removed and handled in covered containers for disposal. Incipient fires should be ringed with a dam of dry nonreactive material or Class D powder and applied to avoid disturbing dust (to prevent dust clouds). Note that bulk aluminum dust can heat spontaneously when damp, and compatible extinguishing agents should be available in metal-powder and scrap storage areas.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides guidance relevant to handling metal powders and explosive-contaminated wastes. For metal powders it prescribes maintaining relative humidity in the 50–60% range (noting spontaneous-ignition hazard above 60%) and using non-sparking tools; it also emphasizes grounding/bonding practices elsewhere in the text. Workstation controls include limiting on-hand material to a 4-hour supply and keeping bulk materials in closed containers. Waste handling requires covered receptacles at each station, daily (or more frequent) removal of contaminated wastes (including rags and empty containers), and disposal of such wastes "in the same manner as deteriorated explosives" by burning at a secluded, well-safeguarded burn site. Burn-site requirements include minimum distances from buildings/highways, barricades, a nearby blasting shelter, clearing combustibles within a 700-foot radius, lining the pit with combustible material soaked in No.2 fuel oil, burning only one type of explosive at a time, and using a fuse. For liquid handling, sumps/collection trays should prevent carryover; wastewater exiting the sump may require chemical treatment to degrade partly soluble explosives, and fully water-soluble explosives should not be allowed into drainage and should be collected by dry methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes grounding and static-control practices for dust collection systems relevant to combustible dust hazards. Key points: filters should have integral grounding straps providing a grounding path to the tubesheet; all component materials must be conductive and nonconductive duct materials (eg, plastic) should be avoided; flexible hoses should be molded with grounding wires that are clamped to upstream and downstream metal ducts. Grounding should include the collector, duct sections, exhaust fan and fan motor. Grounding wires should be plainly visible to operators for quick inspection, and the resistance to ground in grounding wires should be routinely checked and kept below 106 ohms. The excerpt cites NFPA 77 (Recommended Practice on Static Electricity) for further guidance on using grounding to minimize electrostatic hazards, and references NFPA 499 for hazardous-area electrical classification as well as NFPA 68 and NFPA 69 for explosion venting/suppression methods. These practices support elimination of ignition sources and proper electrical classification/installation in combustible-dust environments.

contexts.context: The excerpt contains several points relevant to control of combustible-dust hazards that inform requirements for vacuum cleaning and dust collection practice. It stresses that MIE and MIT testing is useful to identify ignition-source hazards and that test results support prevention measures including removal of ignition sources, grounding and bonding, and control of process/surface temperatures. The text notes inerting as a mitigation strategy but warns that inerting can introduce new hazards, including electrostatic discharge (specifically when CO2 is drawn from high‑pressure or cryogenic tanks) and the potential introduction of ignition sources from inerting equipment such as vacuum pumps. It also describes how secondary dust explosions arise from dispersion of dust layers by energetic disturbances and highlights unsafe housekeeping practices (e.g., vigorous sweeping; cleaning with compressed air) that promote dispersion. These points collectively bear on portable vacuum design/use: control of static, grounding/bonding, elimination of ignition sources, and safe containment/handling of collected dust to prevent dispersion and secondary explosions.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides practical grounding and bonding measures relevant to portable vacuum/dust-collection equipment and containers. It recommends grounding filter bags (Figure 11.1) using embedded braided copper wire (example: 45.7 cm/18") sewn into the bag tops and looping to the tube sheet/cage, and using metal nozzles as conductive paths. Anti-static bags can dissipate charge but may affect filtration. Bonding details include flanged and coupling connections, jumper ground cables (example: 3.17 mm/1/8" dia × 22.9 cm/9"), and flexible ground connections between grounded components. Maintenance actions to ensure conductivity include replacing carbon steel fasteners with 304 stainless steel and removing paint from contact surfaces. For performance, continuous all-metal grounding paths should have resistance less than 10 Ω. Personnel grounding is required where flammable atmospheres or explosive dust clouds with MIE < 30 mJ exist. Use electrical equipment rated for hazardous locations and perform NFPA 70 (Article 500) area classification. For ignition prevention, an inline spark arrestor upstream of a collector is recommended with an expected pressure drop of 0.5–1.0 in. wg.

contexts.question:
Context: We are setting up a Nilfisk CFM 118EXP explosion-proof industrial vacuum cleaner for collecting combustible/reactive metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg and elemental Si, typical particle size 20–63 µm with sub-micron fines). The vacuum already has, or will have installed:
- Antistatic main filter (Nilfisk PN 40000460, 99.7% @ 1.5 µm)
- Upstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631 / 1408678500, 99.97% @ 0.3 µm)
- Downstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631)
- OEM antistatic 1.5" hose with grounded cuffs, conductive metal wand and crevice tool, full grounding chain to building earth

Vacuum is CSA-rated Class I Group D and Class II Groups E, F, G (combustible metal dust). Spec follows NFPA 484 (Combustible Metals) and NFPA 652/660 (Combustible Dust).

The OEM Nilfisk dust collection bag (PN 107413584, the only model confirmed by a Nilfisk distributor to fit the 118EXP collection container) is paper/fleece based and not explicitly antistatic. A previous attempt to buy bags via Grainger (Nilfisk Vacuum Bag 4RYH6 fleece) was identified as non-antistatic and rejected.

Question 1 (primary): For combustible metal powder collection (AlSi10Mg, Si) in an explosion-proof industrial vacuum, is it acceptable per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 / NFPA 660 / OSHA / ATEX consensus practice to operate WITHOUT a disposable collection bag and instead rely on:
(a) the antistatic main filter + upstream HEPA + downstream HEPA already installed, AND
(b) an antistatic / conductive polyethylene liner placed inside the stainless-steel collection bin (electrically bonded to the bin / vacuum body so the grounding chain is preserved)?

Specifically address:
- Whether conductive (10^4 – 10^6 Ω surface resistivity) or static-dissipative (10^6 – 10^11 Ω) liners satisfy NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 grounding and static-control requirements for combustible metal dust collection,
- Whether the absence of a bag introduces unacceptable risks (powder fluidization, filter blinding, dust resuspension during emptying, MIE-related ignition hazards) that a bag would otherwise mitigate,
- Whether collected metal powder in a liner can be safely disposed of / transferred to an outer waste container, and what NFPA 484 says about temporary storage of reactive metal fines,
- Any documented industry guidance from Nilfisk, Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, or similar manufacturers about bag-vs-liner-vs-bagless for AlSi10Mg / aluminum / silicon powder.

Question 2 (secondary, sourcing): If a true antistatic / conductive disposable filter bag IS required (not just a liner), please identify specific commercial part numbers that:
- Fit the Nilfisk CFM 118EXP collection container (~12.5" / 320 mm internal diameter container, sized to nest in the stainless drum used on 118 EXP and A15EXP models),
- Are explicitly rated antistatic / conductive (carbon-loaded paper, conductive plastic, or antistatic-treated fleece) and suitable for combustible metal dust per NFPA 484,
- Are available from a US supplier (Nilfisk direct, Fisher Scientific, Grainger, Caliber Equipment, SweepScrub, IndustrialVacs, etc.) with a sourceable link or distributor contact.

Note that Nilfisk technical support has told us this 118EXP model is old enough that it is no longer fully supported and they cannot definitively confirm parts compatibility, so primary literature, NFPA standards interpretation, and cross-referencing alternative manufacturer (Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, Hafco) combustible-metal-dust accessories are particularly valuable. The serial-number sticker shows "L" prefix per Nilfisk telephone guidance.

Please cite NFPA standards by section number where possible, and provide direct product URLs for any recommended bags/liners.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general principles relevant to dust explosion parameters that would apply when assessing silicon powder clouds. Smaller particles are more explosive: they disperse more easily, stay airborne longer, require lower ignition energy, lower minimum ignition temperature, and tend to lower minimum explosive concentration (MEC); however, for very fine particles MEC can become independent of size. Particle size also affects maximum overpressure (Pmax) and maximum pressure rise rate (dp/dt)max; extremely fine reactive dusts have produced Pmax values up to 26 bar. Kst is not an intrinsic constant for a substance — it depends on test apparatus shape, ignition energy, dispersion system, time delays and turbulence. A dust cloud must be within a definite concentration range to explode, and at concentrations below the minimum there is insufficient heat to propagate flame. Moisture generally reduces explosibility and ignition sensitivity (examples show dried samples may be explosive while undried are not). Common ignition sources include hot surfaces, welding/cutting, electrical/static sparks, lightning and shock waves. These factors (particle size, concentration, moisture, ignition energy and test conditions) control MIE, Kst and Pmax for any dust, including silicon.

snippets: As the particle size of dust decreases, there is an increase in the explosiveness [31].
Smaller dust particles require lower energy and will reduce the minimum concentration and the minimum temperature of ignition.
For very fine particles, the minimum explosive concentration (MEC) is independent of size.
Extremely fine and reactive dust can reach an overpressure of 26 bar, which could alter the quasi-detonative combustion transition [34].
Kst is not a value inherent to the substance because it varies based on the shape of the test instrument, ignition energy, time delays, and dispersion system that affect the turbulence degree.
The dust in the air mixture is required to be within a definite range of concentration for a dust explosion to occur.
Typically, the explosibility of materials decreases at higher content of moisture.

Mintz [39] performed an explosion test on dried and undried corn starch at particle sizes from 120 μm to 150 μm. It was found that the dried sample became explosive and the undried sample could not be exploded for very fine dust, which confirms that moisture content is an important influence.
Other dust explosion triggers are electrical and static sparks, lightning and shock waves [28].

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses general tendencies and caveats about nanoparticle dust explosion hazards that are relevant when considering any specific powder (such as silicon). Extrapolation suggests nm-particle clouds could show very low MIEs and high explosion violence, but several mitigating factors apply: forming well-dispersed nanoparticle clouds in industry is extremely difficult due to strong cohesion, and rapid coagulation/agglomeration will enlarge particles within fractions of a second. Laboratory tests (with ignition delays ~20–60 ms) may overestimate industrial ignition sensitivity because real accidental delays are often longer. Empirical results show nm-particle clouds do not exhibit larger KSt than micron powders, although some metals (and a few organics and sulphur) have reported MIEs <1 mJ. Very low-energy sparks can arise from small capacitances or moderate voltages (example: 20 pF at 1 kV stores ~0.01 mJ), and electrostatic induction (e.g., tramp metal entering charged powder fields) or mechanical impact/friction can produce ignition. The excerpt does not provide specific numeric MIE, KSt or Pmax values for silicon powder, but it outlines mechanisms and considerations that strongly influence those parameters for nanopowders.

snippets: So far indications of MIEs << 1 mJ of nm-particle dust clouds in air only exist for metals.
With C = 20 pF, and U = 1 kV, the stored energy ½CU2 = 0.01 mJ, which might be of the order of the MIEs of some very spark-ignition sensitive dust.
Laboratory-scale experiments have shown that nm-particle dust clouds of given materials do not have any larger KSt-values than clouds of µm-particle powders.
The MIE values of some metals are lower for dust clouds of nm primary particles than for clouds of µm primary particles.

MIEs < 1 mJ have also been reported for some synthetic organic powders and sulphur, but it is not clear whether this is due to very small primary-particles sizes, or to highly reactive chemical compositions.

a)  Formation of clouds of well-dispersed primary particles from bulk powders consisting of nm-particles is extremely difficult to achieve by dust dispersion processes normally operating in the process industries, due to the strong inter-particle cohesion forces.
b)  Should perfect dispersion nevertheless become a reality, extremely fast coagulation will transform the primary particles into much larger agglomerates within fractions of a second.
2. The delay between the moment of formation of a well-dispersed nm-particle dust cloud and the moment of ignition of the cloud is decisive for the extent of coagulation.

With regard to ignition by mechanical friction/impact the findings by Wu et al. [19] indicate that careful precautions have to be taken to prevent ignition of clouds in air of some nm-particle metal powders by heat from mechanical impact of friction.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses mechanisms and trends relevant to dust explosions for metals and carbon, but does not provide silicon-specific MIE, KSt or Pmax values. It outlines three stages controlling flame propagation and notes that for particles below ~10 µm particle-size effects on burning rate become negligible because gas-phase combustion limits the rate. For metals (including aluminium and magnesium) combustion occurs at or near the particle surface, so ignition sensitivity and explosibility tend to increase as primary-particle size decreases down to the nm-range. However, rapid coagulation (example: with K = 0.5·10^-9 cm3/s particle counts can fall to ~10^9 cm^-3 within 1 s) and surface oxidation can limit or reverse increased explosibility at the genuine nanoparticle scale. The MEC for organics is ~100 g/m3; for metals MEC is generally higher and roughly scales with particle density. Laboratory dispersion methods trigger ignition 20–60 ms after dispersion, so coagulation may be limited in those tests. Example data for aluminium nanopowders (100–210 nm) show high Pmax and dP/dt (e.g., 12.5 bar, 1677 bar/s, KSt 449 at 210 nm), illustrating trends for metals but not supplying silicon-specific parameters.

snippets: For smaller particles than the order of 10 µm, τd and τm are negligible compared to τc and particle size has no longer any influence on the burning rate, which is essentially limited by the rate of gas phase combustion.
In the case of pure carbon and various metals including aluminium and magnesium, the combustion process mainly occurs at or near the particle surface.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides guidance on how to assess dust explosion properties and how test results should be interpreted, but does not give specific numeric MIE, Kst or Pmax values for silicon. Key points: MEC (minimum explosible concentration) for powders is reported typically as 15–60 gm/m3 (with very high reported concentrations up to 2000–6000 gm/m3 for dense clouds), and MEC should be measured using the ASTM E-1515 apparatus rather than less severe tests. PMAX and Kst are measured per ASTM E-1226 and are used for equipment design and venting. Minimum ignition energy (MIE) is highly sensitive to particle size—scaling roughly with the 2nd–3rd power of representative particle diameter—so samples should represent the worst credible fine fraction (commonly sub-200 mesh or finer). Use of an appropriate igniter energy (e.g., 2.5 J or larger chamber) is recommended to avoid underestimating MEC. Special considerations include freshly milled metals having unusually low ignition energies and rapid surface oxidation, and the need to evaluate hybrid mixtures if volatile content exceeds ~0.2–0.5 wt%. For silicon-specific parameters, dedicated tests or authoritative data sources are required.

Metal dusts (e.g., Al, Mg, Zr, Ti) have high heats of combustion and very hot burning particles; thermal radiation can play a central role in flame propagation and can even ignite nearby clouds (Leuschke 1965). Explosion violence is characterized by the maximum rate of pressure rise measured in closed-bomb tests and 1 m3-type vessels; (dP/dt)max from such tests is used to assess violence (Kst is derived from these dynamic-pressure measurements in standard vessels). Dust chemistry (e.g., halogens) and particle size strongly affect combustion rate, Pmax and (dP/dt)max. Moisture markedly reduces ignition sensitivity and explosion violence; its effect on MIE is stronger than on minimum ignition temperature. Added inert particles can influence flame speed via flow/turbulence and radiative effects. These points indicate what influences silicon dust parameters and what test methods and variables to consult when seeking specific MIE, Kst and Pmax data for silicon powder.

NFPA-654 also treats very thin deposits as de minimis: users need not count layers thinner than 1/64 in. (or where surface color is discernible) when totaling accumulation. The excerpt provides a worked example: for a dust with bulk density 75 lb/ft3, a hazard exists if total accumulation exceeds 1,000 ft2 × 1/32 in., roughly 375 in3 (2.6 ft3). This text does not include housekeeping frequency, container emptying intervals, or specific timing/inspection schedules; those requirements are not present on the provided pages.

Historically, NFPA 654 referenced a 1/32 in. dust layer criterion ("A 1/32 in. criterion, adjusted for bulk density, had been referenced by NFPA 654,") though analyses indicate this may be overly conservative for some dusts. contexts.context: The excerpt states NFPA 654 uses a default layer depth criterion of 1/32 in. based on a bulk density of 75 lb/ft3, and explicitly permits adjusting the allowable thickness for materials with lower bulk density via the equation relocated in the TIA to Section 6.1. The product of allowable thickness and bulk density corresponds to an allowable mass per unit area of 0.195 lb/ft2 (for the 1/32 in. at 75 lb/ft3 basis). Related standards use different numeric values derived from the same mass-based concept (for example, NFPA 664 lists 1/8 in. assuming 20 lb/ft3; NFPA 61 references lower bulk density for grain). The standard and the TIA emphasize that the criterion applies generally to exposed surfaces (not just floors or mitigation-by-separation situations) and that common misinterpretations include ignoring layers on equipment or assuming a clean floor provides separation. The excerpt does not provide an explicit housekeeping frequency or a specific requirement for how often collected combustible dust must be emptied from containers; NFPA-484 is noted as not allowing accumulation and “infers daily cleaning schedule,” but NFPA-654’s text on container emptying frequency is not included in the excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses NFPA 654 layer-depth criteria and the TIA amendments for evaluating dust hazard areas. Historically, NFPA 654 paragraph 6.2.3.1 identified a 1/32 in. (0.8 mm) dust accumulation threshold for areas where separation is used to limit hazardous areas. The TIA-amended entry to Section 6.1 requires evaluation of process/facility areas where dust accumulations exist, but exempts surfaces where the dust layer depth is 1/64 in. or less or where underlying surface color is readily discernible. For deciding a dust-hazardous area, the standard uses area/volume thresholds: for general footprints, dust accumulation exceeding the layer-depth criterion over more than 5% of the footprint, or total accumulated volume exceeding (layer depth × 5% footprint) constitutes a hazard; for footprints ≥20,000 ft2 the corresponding numeric thresholds are >1,000 ft2 or volume > (layer depth × 1,000 ft2). The paper emphasizes that very thin layers (e.g., 1/100 in. for cornstarch) can be entrained and propagate burning clouds, so thin accumulations may still be hazardous. The excerpt does not state housekeeping frequencies or container emptying intervals.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that residual material from extinguished metal-powder/solvent-wetted aluminum fires must be allowed to cool to ambient temperature and, after confirming no hot spots, be carefully removed for disposal and "handled in covered containers." Fire-extinguishing agents compatible with the specific metal hazards should be provided in metal-scrap and metal-powder storage areas. Application of Class D (dry powder) agents should be done with minimum disturbance to avoid creating a dust cloud; spark-proof tools (e.g., scoop or shovel) are recommended when applying graphite-based powders. Several common extinguishing agents (water, foams, Halon, CO2, nitrogen in many cases, Halon replacements, and ABC/BC dry chemical extinguishers) are explicitly not recommended for combustible-metal fires. The text describes graphite and sodium chloride as common Class D agents and gives practical handling guidance, but it does not provide NFPA 484’s explicit container specifications (e.g., material, grounding/bonding, or exact temporary-storage container type) nor detailed conductive vs non-conductive container requirements. For those specifics the excerpt directs users to NFPA guidance, MSDS, and referenced standards.

The application of the dry extinguishing agent should be conducted in such a manner as to avoid any disturbance of the combustible-metal dust, which could cause a dust cloud.

The following agents are not recommended by experts to be used as extinguishing agents on combustible-metal fires because of adverse reac-tions or ineffectiveness:

One commercial extinguishing agent is Amerex G-Plus Dry Powder7 which is a black, non-toxic material consisting of finely graded, granular graphite (carbon). It is normally applied to a metal fire using a spark proof scoop or shovel. The manufacturer recommends that the powder be applied with a minimum disturbance, adequately covering the fire area to a depth of approximately two inches.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not cite NFPA 484 specifically but provides practical guidance on containers and grounding for powder handling that is relevant to metal dust waste handling. Bags or liners with an internal metal foil can become charged and produce sparks unless specially grounded. Paper bags and chimeless fiber drums are semiconductive above ~10–20% RH and can be grounded by contact with grounded equipment or a grounded operator (if nonconductive gloves are not used). Flexible Intermediate Bulk Containers (FIBCs) are classified as Type A (100% plastic, cannot be grounded), Type B (thin-walled 100% plastic, cannot be grounded), Type C (conductive, require grounding) and Type D (antistatic, do not require grounding). For powders that do not evolve flammable vapors, ungrounded Type A or B may be acceptable if the operator is grounded; Types A/B should not be used where flammable vapor may be present. If ignition-sensitive powders are handled or moisture sensitivity precludes thin-walled bags, Types C or D should be considered. For transfers into flammable-liquid atmospheres, use intermediate grounded metal hoppers and inerting to minimize ignition risk.

A proposed European FIBC classification scheme [152] referring to Type A, B and C containers is used in the following sections. Type D containers have been added to reflect recent developments. In brief, these FIBCs are
Type A. General 100% plastic types that cannot be grounded.
Type B. Thin-walled 100% plastic types that cannot be grounded.
Type C. Conductive types that require grounding and,
Type D. Antistatic types that do not require grounding.

If a powder is capable of evolving flammable vapor at or above its LFL it should be considered as being handled in a flammable vapor atmosphere
Types A and B should not be used in flammable vapor atmospheres.

If the risk of Type A is seen to be unacceptable, for example if an ignition sensitive or toxic dust is being handled, and Type B cannot be used owing to moisture sensitivity, Types C or D should be considered instead

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses carbon-loaded (carbon-filled) conductive plastics used as IC carriers and other ESD protective items. It emphasizes that carbon loading — and therefore conductivity — varies by supplier, and that triboelectric charge generation also varies with manufacturer and device type. High bulk conductivity does not guarantee low triboelectric charging; in fact, carbon-filled tubes can transfer charge effectively to devices as they leave the tube, so personnel must use wrist straps to avoid inadvertent charging of ICs. Antistat-treated plastics and antistat-impregnated plastics do not provide effective shielding from external electrostatic fields, and topical antistat coatings lose effectiveness with use. For tote boxes/bins/trays the material should be conductive enough to prevent significant induced voltages but not so conductive as to permit spark discharges. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses properties and limitations of carbon-loaded polyolefins and conductive plastics relevant to ESD protective packaging. Carbon-loaded polyolefins can abrade and deposit black carbonaceous dust, making them unsuitable for many clean-room environments; antistat-impregnated plastics may wear out as antistat additives deplete. Carbon-filled plastics in contact with aluminum and salt water have been shown to produce EMFs (up to +3 V) that can cause corrosion. For protective packaging, three principles are emphasized: equipotential bonding (e.g., conductive foam, shorting plugs or shunts on edge connectors to keep circuitry at the same potential), reduction of triboelectric charging (choose compatible materials, use conductive packing to bleed charges rapidly, or use surface contaminants/antistats to reduce contact charging), and Faraday-cage shielding (conductive bags shield internal devices from external fields). The excerpt does not provide numerical surface resistivity values, specific ESD S541 classifications, MIL-PRF-81705 Type III details, or commercial size/specification listings for carbon-loaded black polyethylene bags.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes protective bag types relevant to carbon-loaded conductive (black) polyethylene bags. It notes that "bulk conductive plastic bags typically are black and are carbon filled to obtain the necessary conductivity," and that such bags (and other antistatic bags) generally provide protection against triboelectric charging. However, bag types differ in their ability to shield external electrostatic fields: some only protect against triboelectric charging, others only against external fields, and some against both. MIL-B-81705 Type I and Type II bags are individually incomplete (Type I: good field protection, no tribocharging protection; Type II: tribocharging protection, no field protection); the paper states a Type III bag combining both features is needed. None of the bags provide true equipotential bonding, so a separate shunt bar or shorting connector is recommended when inserting PCBs or modules. Antistat-impregnated plastics rely on surface moisture, degrade at low humidity, and can show large increases in surface resistivity after prolonged air exposure (orders-of-magnitude changes after ~1 year). The excerpt does not contain numerical surface resistivity values, specific ESD S541 classification entries, the detailed MIL-PRF-81705 Type III specification text, nor commercial size/spec tables—those would need to be obtained from standards documents or manufacturer datasheets.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses metal oxide inerting as a method to reduce explosion hazards from metal dusts, including aluminum. Studies show that introducing metal oxides like Al2O3 can reduce flame speed in aluminum dust clouds by approximately 40% with 10 wt% oxide content, and coating zirconium particles with iron oxide reduces flame velocity. However, the text notes significant limitations: certain inertant materials like monoammonium phosphate and sodium bicarbonate proved ineffective at inerting aluminum ignition even at high concentrations. The excerpt also identifies a key practical disadvantage—customers are typically unwilling to contaminate their product with inert materials during storage. While the excerpt addresses metal oxide interactions with metal dusts, it does not directly address thermite reaction hazards or cross-contamination risks during handling of multiple reactive metal powders.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DOE occurrence report (ID--LITC-TOWN-1995-0002) documenting a thermite reaction hazard involving aluminum and copper oxide powders. A laboratory technician sustained minor burns when approximately 50 grams of aluminum and copper oxide powders (325-mesh, 44 micron) ignited inside a 250 ml polyethylene bottle during mixing. The investigation revealed critical factors: the bottle was only 10% full (compared to usual 50-70% fill level), and the shaking process may have been more aggressive than typical. The ignition mechanism involved aluminum dust reacting with air in the bottle headspace, generating heat that subsequently triggered the aluminum-copper oxide thermite reaction. Static electrical discharge was identified as the probable ignition source. This incident illustrates hazards of handling reactive metal powder mixtures, including thermite compound instability, dust cloud formation, and electrostatic ignition risks during storage and handling operations.

contexts.context: This paper investigates electrical conduction and dielectric breakdown in aluminum oxide (Al2O3) insulators on silicon. The authors fabricated metal-insulator-silicon (MIS) capacitors with Al2O3 oxide layers formed by oxidizing AlN films at temperatures ranging from 800-1100°C. The dielectric constants measured for the thermally oxidized Al2O3 ranged from 3 to 9, which is lower than the dielectric constant of sapphire (α-Al2O3) at 10.6, likely due to differences in microstructure and density. Current-voltage measurements were performed to characterize the dielectric breakdown strength and electrical conduction mechanisms. The paper also reports on oxide defect densities measured through capacitance-voltage characteristics, with well-oxidized samples showing defect densities below 10¹¹ cm⁻² eV⁻¹, comparable to device-grade SiO2.

contexts.context: This paper reports on aluminum oxide (Al2O3) insulators produced by thermally oxidizing AlN films on silicon substrates. Key electrical properties measured include: resistivity greater than 10^12 Ω-cm at 0.3 MV/cm electric field with leakage current density less than 10^-7 A cm^-2; critical dielectric breakdown field strength ranging from 4 to 5 MV/cm; and dielectric constant ranging from 3 to 9. The best electrical properties were obtained when all AlN was fully oxidized to Al2O3 with no residual AlN. The conduction mechanism was identified as Frenkel-Poole emission. The study notes that aluminum oxide produced by thermal oxidation is thermally stable and mechanically hard, making it potentially useful for gate dielectric applications in field effect transistors and flash memory circuits due to its higher dielectric constant compared to SiO2.

contexts.context: This excerpt discusses quantitative models of breakdown in anodic aluminum oxide, specifically Ikonopisov's electron avalanche multiplication model and Albella et al.'s improved model. The breakdown potential (UB) depends on the nature of the anodized metal, electrolyte resistivity (ρe), electric field (E), and temperature (T). The initial model proposed that electrons injected from the electrolyte into the oxide conduction band undergo avalanche multiplication, with breakdown occurring when electronic current reaches a critical value. Equations 30 and 36 show mathematical relationships between breakdown potential and various parameters. The improved model by Albella et al. incorporated the effect of electrolyte species into the oxide, proposing that initial electrons come from incorporated electrolyte species acting as impurity centers near the conduction band, releasing electrons via the Poole-Frenkel mechanism. The breakdown potential equals the electric field multiplied by critical oxide thickness (UB = Etox,B).

contexts.context: This peer-reviewed article characterizes aluminum oxide (Al2O3) insulators on silicon through electrical measurements. The aluminum oxide samples exhibited dielectric breakdown at fields ranging from 4 to 5 MV/cm, significantly higher than the accepted value for bulk sapphire (0.5 MV/cm). Leakage current densities were below 1.2 × 10^-12 A/cm² at fields under 0.3 MV/cm, corresponding to resistivities exceeding 10^15 Ω-cm, which agreed reasonably with published values for sapphire. While the dielectric constant is referenced as 3.9 for comparison materials (SiO2), the breakdown field of aluminum oxide was lower than SiO2 (which broke down near 10 MV/cm). However, the authors note that due to aluminum oxide's higher dielectric constant, the actual breakdown voltage in optimized MIS devices could be comparable to SiO2 despite the lower breakdown field strength.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses Glor's criterion for propagating brush discharges on flexible intermediate bulk containers (FIBCs), establishing a 4 kV breakdown voltage threshold below which propagating brushes cannot be produced. It explains that 100% plastic FIBCs with wall breakdown voltages less than 4 kV are immune to propagating brush phenomena, independent of wall thickness. However, achieving a 4 kV breakdown voltage requires limiting liner thickness to approximately 1 mil, which may be inadequate for moisture protection in sensitive products. The excerpt also notes that the relationship between film potential and layer thickness is critical for propagating brush production. For preventing brush discharges, FIBCs must have ground resistance less than 10^8 Ohm and be properly grounded. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses propagating brush discharges (PBDs) on insulating layers over grounded metal substrates. Key findings include a 4 kV threshold below which no discharges were observed on an 80-mm polycarbonate film with brass backing. Between 4-8 kV, charge transfers were minimal and consistent with brush discharges rather than PBDs. A transition region occurred at 8-12 kV where charge transfer increased rapidly, with a tentative 10 mC threshold for PBD definition occurring at 10 kV. Layer thickness affects the electric field gradient across the surface—as thickness increases, capacitance decreases and the electric field component across the surface increases, promoting propagation. Breakdown strength is influenced by material properties and defects; pores and pinholes can reduce breakdown voltage and prevent PBD occurrence. Question: You are following up on a prior task: You are following up on a prior task: You are following up on a prior task: You are following up on a prior task: Context: We are setting up a Nilfisk CFM 118EXP explosion-proof industrial vacuum cleaner for collecting combustible/reactive metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg and elemental Si, typical particle size 20–63 µm with sub-micron fines). The vacuum already has, or will have installed:
- Antistatic main filter (Nilfisk PN 40000460, 99.7% @ 1.5 µm)
- Upstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631 / 1408678500, 99.97% @ 0.3 µm)
- Downstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631)
- OEM antistatic 1.5" hose with grounded cuffs, conductive metal wand and crevice tool, full grounding chain to building earth

Vacuum is CSA-rated Class I Group D and Class II Groups E, F, G (combustible metal dust). Spec follows NFPA 484 (Combustible Metals) and NFPA 652/660 (Combustible Dust).

The OEM Nilfisk dust collection bag (PN 107413584, the only model confirmed by a Nilfisk distributor to fit the 118EXP collection container) is paper/fleece based and not explicitly antistatic. A previous attempt to buy bags via Grainger (Nilfisk Vacuum Bag 4RYH6 fleece) was identified as non-antistatic and rejected.

Question 1 (primary): For combustible metal powder collection (AlSi10Mg, Si) in an explosion-proof industrial vacuum, is it acceptable per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 / NFPA 660 / OSHA / ATEX consensus practice to operate WITHOUT a disposable collection bag and instead rely on:
(a) the antistatic main filter + upstream HEPA + downstream HEPA already installed, AND
(b) an antistatic / conductive polyethylene liner placed inside the stainless-steel collection bin (electrically bonded to the bin / vacuum body so the grounding chain is preserved)?

Specifically address:
- Whether conductive (10^4 – 10^6 Ω surface resistivity) or static-dissipative (10^6 – 10^11 Ω) liners satisfy NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 grounding and static-control requirements for combustible metal dust collection,
- Whether the absence of a bag introduces unacceptable risks (powder fluidization, filter blinding, dust resuspension during emptying, MIE-related ignition hazards) that a bag would otherwise mitigate,
- Whether collected metal powder in a liner can be safely disposed of / transferred to an outer waste container, and what NFPA 484 says about temporary storage of reactive metal fines,
- Any documented industry guidance from Nilfisk, Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, or similar manufacturers about bag-vs-liner-vs-bagless for AlSi10Mg / aluminum / silicon powder.

Question 2 (secondary, sourcing): If a true antistatic / conductive disposable filter bag IS required (not just a liner), please identify specific commercial part numbers that:
- Fit the Nilfisk CFM 118EXP collection container (~12.5" / 320 mm internal diameter container, sized to nest in the stainless drum used on 118 EXP and A15EXP models),
- Are explicitly rated antistatic / conductive (carbon-loaded paper, conductive plastic, or antistatic-treated fleece) and suitable for combustible metal dust per NFPA 484,
- Are available from a US supplier (Nilfisk direct, Fisher Scientific, Grainger, Caliber Equipment, SweepScrub, IndustrialVacs, etc.) with a sourceable link or distributor contact.

Note that Nilfisk technical support has told us this 118EXP model is old enough that it is no longer fully supported and they cannot definitively confirm parts compatibility, so primary literature, NFPA standards interpretation, and cross-referencing alternative manufacturer (Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, Hafco) combustible-metal-dust accessories are particularly valuable. The serial-number sticker shows "L" prefix per Nilfisk telephone guidance.

Please cite NFPA standards by section number where possible, and provide direct product URLs for any recommended bags/liners.

1. **Empty-daily clarification.** What exactly should be emptied daily — the conductive PE liner inside the vacuum collection bin, or the outer grounded steel pail that the sealed liner is transferred into for transport / interim storage? Cite NFPA 484, NFPA 652, OSHA 1910, or related guidance for the time/quantity threshold. Is the "daily" cadence quantitative (e.g. based on a max accumulation mass or layer depth such as 1/32" per NFPA 654 housekeeping)? In a low-duty research lab generating, say, only tens of grams of AlSi10Mg / Si powder per week (not continuous production), is daily emptying still required, or is a fill-level / volume / time threshold (e.g. <25 % of bin, or weekly when contaminated) defensible?

# Verification of Nilfisk CFM 118EXP Crevice Tool Ground-Continuity Anomaly

---

## CLAIM 1: MEASUREMENT INTERPRETATION

**Verdict: CORRECT**

The "OL on REL-locked low range, megohms with autoranging" behavior is a genuine reading of a high surface resistance (≥ 10⁶ Ω), not a meter artifact. A standard bench DMM applies an open-circuit test voltage of typically 0.5–3 V on its resistance ranges. Aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) — the material produced by anodization — is a high-quality dielectric insulator with the following measured properties:

- **Resistivity**: > 10¹² Ω·cm at moderate electric fields, with leakage current densities < 10⁻⁷ A/cm² at 0.3 MV/cm (kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 1-2). Published values for sapphire (crystalline Al₂O₃) exceed 10¹⁵ Ω·cm (kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 3-5).
- **Dielectric breakdown field strength**: 4–5 MV/cm for thermally produced Al₂O₃ (kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 1-2, kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 3-5). For a typical sulfuric-acid clear anodize layer of 5–25 µm thickness, this corresponds to a **breakdown voltage of 200–1,250 V** — orders of magnitude above any DMM test voltage.
- **Dielectric constant**: 3–9 depending on crystallinity and processing (kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 2-3, kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 5-6).

A few-nanometer **native oxide** (the natural Al₂O₃ that forms spontaneously on all aluminum in air) is only ~2–5 nm thick. At a breakdown field of ~5 MV/cm, a 5 nm native oxide breaks down at ~2.5 V — easily pierced by a DMM's test voltage and by normal probe pressure. An engineered anodize layer is **1,000–5,000× thicker** than native oxide and therefore cannot be penetrated by the DMM. The fact that **light scratching does not restore conductivity** is diagnostic: anodize (Mohs ~9, Vickers ~400–600 HV) is harder than the underlying aluminum alloy (Mohs ~2.5–3), so a fingernail, probe drag, or light abrasion does not reach bright metal. This is pathognomonic of an engineered dielectric coating, not native oxide or machining oil.

**Your reading is real. The crevice tool surface is insulating at ≥ 10⁶ Ω.**

---

## CLAIM 2: IS IT ANODIZED?

**Verdict: CORRECT — most likely explanation, though no specific documentation of the 01768900 finish was found**

The symptom set — solid aluminum alloy body, silvery/clear metallic appearance identical to the bare-aluminum wand, megohm surface resistance surviving light scratches, and a Nilfisk support representative describing it as "just aluminum" — is fully consistent with **Type II sulfuric-acid clear (natural) anodize** per MIL-A-8625F. Clear anodize is transparent, preserves the metallic appearance, is the most common commercial anodize process for aluminum, and produces the exact dielectric behavior observed.

No documentation of the 01768900 crevice tool's specified finish was found in any retrieved literature, patent, or manufacturer database. Nilfisk's own technical support did not identify the finish. **The literature is silent on this specific part number's surface treatment.** However, the following reasoning strongly favors anodize over alternatives:

- **Bare mill aluminum with native oxide only**: Would show < 1 Ω surface resistance under probe pressure. Eliminated by the megohm reading.
- **Carbon-loaded static-dissipative plastic that looks metallic**: Possible in theory, but the user has confirmed the part is unambiguously solid metal (machined aluminum), not plastic. Eliminated.
- **Conductive coating over aluminum** (e.g., nickel plating, chromate conversion): Would show low resistance. Eliminated.
- **Clear anodize**: Matches all observations. This is the most likely explanation by exclusion.

It is plausible that Nilfisk anodizes the crevice tool for corrosion protection and abrasion resistance (reasonable for a tool that contacts hard surfaces) without considering the static-control implication, or that the tool was designed for non-EXP applications and is shared across product lines.

---

## CLAIM 3: IS AN ANODIZED EXP TOOL A DEFECT / CONTRADICTION?

**Verdict: CORRECT-WITH-CAVEAT — the anodize itself is not necessarily a hazard IF the tool body is properly bonded to ground through the joint, but the as-supplied failure to bond IS a non-conformance**

### 3a. Isolated-conductor hazard

An electrically conductive mass (aluminum crevice tool) that is **insulated from ground** by a dielectric coating is the textbook definition of an **isolated conductor** — a recognized ignition hazard in combustible-dust environments. Charge can accumulate on the isolated conductor from triboelectric contact with powder, and the stored energy can discharge as an incendive spark when the conductor approaches a grounded surface or the operator. All metal components in the airstream path must be electrically bonded and grounded; metal components must not be allowed to act as isolated capacitors (comer2020explosionventedequipment pages 140-146).

### 3b. Propagating brush discharge (PBD) from the anodize layer

Once the tool body is properly **bonded to ground through a clean metal-to-metal joint at the socket**, the question becomes: is the anodize layer on the outer surface itself a PBD hazard?

The established criterion is that propagating brush discharges cannot be produced when the wall breakdown voltage is below **4 kV** (Glor's criterion) (britton1993statichazardsusing pages 10-12, britton2010avoidingstaticignition pages 53-56). For sulfuric-acid clear anodize:

- Typical thickness: 5–25 µm
- Breakdown field: ~4–5 MV/cm (kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 1-2, kolodzey2000electricalconductionand pages 3-5)
- Breakdown voltage at 25 µm: ~100–125 V; at 5 µm: ~20–25 V

These breakdown voltages are **far below the 4 kV PBD threshold**. Therefore, even if the anodize layer is fully insulating, its breakdown voltage (~20–125 V) is well below 4 kV, meaning **propagating brush discharges cannot develop on it**. Any charge deposited on the outer anodize surface will punch through the thin dielectric and drain to the grounded aluminum substrate before reaching PBD-capable potentials.

**Conclusion**: A tens-of-microns anodized skin over **grounded** aluminum is NOT a PBD hazard. The anodize is too thin to support the 4 kV potential needed for PBD. The only real requirement is that the assembled tool not float — i.e., the aluminum body must be bonded to ground through the socket joint (britton2010avoidingstaticignition pages 53-56).

### 3b (AS-SUPPLIED FAILURE)

**Verdict: CORRECT — this is a non-conforming condition**

The OEM manual (UL 1213 par. 22) requires ≤ 0.1 Ω tool-to-wand before each use. The crevice tool reads **open** at the socket joint as supplied. This means:

1. The tool fails the OEM's own acceptance criterion.
2. If used as-supplied, the tool body would be an isolated conductor in the airstream — an ignition hazard in a Class II hazardous location.
3. This is an out-of-spec / non-conforming condition for a tool sold as part of an EXP-certified system.

**Defensible courses of action** (in order of preference):
1. **Contact Nilfisk industrial vacuum division** (callback pending) and request either (a) a confirmed-conductive replacement crevice tool, or (b) written confirmation that the anodized tool is intended to bond through its socket when properly seated.
2. **Field-remediate the joint** per Claim 5 below, documented in the DHA.
3. **Replace** with a confirmed-conductive third-party crevice tool of the same diameter.

---

## CLAIM 4: GOVERNING ACCEPTANCE CRITERION

**Verdict: CORRECT-WITH-CAVEAT — the 0.1 Ω figure is a per-connection UL 1213 criterion, but the conductive hose is a different class of component**

The OEM manual's ≤ 0.1 Ω criterion (UL 1213 par. 22) applies to **metal-to-metal connections** — tool to wand, wand to coupler, coupler to inlet. These are hard-metal joints where 0.1 Ω is achievable and verifiable.

The conductive hose is a fundamentally different component: a polymer tube with embedded conductive elements (carbon loading and/or wire helix). Its specification is R ≤ 10⁴ Ω (manufacturer-confirmed), and the measured ~4 Ω is well within that spec. This is consistent with NFPA 77 guidance that grounding resistance should be routinely checked and kept below 10⁶ Ω for grounding wires, with < 10 Ω for continuous all-metal ground paths (johnson2008designingyourdust pages 7-8, comer2020explosionventedequipment pages 140-146).

**Reconciliation**: The 0.1 Ω criterion applies **per metal-to-metal connection**. The hose is not a metal-to-metal connection — it is a listed conductive component with its own resistance specification. The correct interpretation is:

| Connection | Criterion | Your Reading | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tool → wand (metal-to-metal) | ≤ 0.1 Ω per UL 1213 | Dust brush: 0.03 Ω; Crevice: OPEN | Brush PASS; Crevice FAIL |
| Wand → coupler (metal-to-metal) | ≤ 0.1 Ω | < 0.1 Ω | PASS |
| Hose end-to-end (conductive polymer) | ≤ 10⁴ Ω per manufacturer spec; < 10 Ω per NFPA 77 bonded-system criterion | ~4 Ω | PASS |
| Bin/body → building ground | < 1 Ω (metal-to-metal) | < 1 Ω | PASS |
| Liner → ground (conductive polymer contact) | < 1 kΩ (per Britton guidance for conductive objects near powder) | < 1 kΩ measured | PASS |

**A 4 Ω conductive hose does NOT violate the 0.1 Ω per-connection criterion** because the hose is not a "connection" in the UL 1213 sense — it is a listed conductive component with bulk resistance. Your system passes at every point except the crevice tool joint.

---

## CLAIM 5: REMEDIATION

**Verdict: CORRECT-WITH-CAVEAT**

The correct fix is to **bond the joint** (restore metal-to-metal contact at the socket interface), NOT to strip the entire tool.

### Recommended diagnostic sequence (before any abrasion):

1. **Check for anodize rack marks**: The anodizing process requires electrical contact to the part. There are typically small uncoated spots where the anodizing rack touched the part — often inside the bore, on internal flats, or at sharp edges. Probe these locations with the DMM. If you find a bare-metal spot reading < 0.1 Ω inside the socket bore, the tool may bond when fully seated on the wand with firm pressure.

2. **Confirm full tight seating**: Push the crevice tool fully onto the wand with firm hand pressure. The socket bore may have a tighter interference fit that scrapes through the anodize. Re-measure at full seating.

3. **Contact cleaner**: Apply plastic-safe electronic contact cleaner (e.g., CRC QD Contact Cleaner) to the socket bore and the wand tip, seat firmly, and re-measure. This removes any oil film but will not penetrate anodize.

4. **Fine non-metallic abrasion of mating surfaces ONLY**: If the above fail, use a fine non-metallic Scotch-Brite pad (gray or maroon, NOT green — green is too aggressive) to lightly abrade **only the inner bore of the crevice tool socket** and the mating section of the wand tip. The goal is to break through the anodize layer at the contact band (~5–10 mm) where the tool seats on the wand. This is a minimal, targeted intervention.

5. **Re-verify**: After seating, the tool-to-wand resistance must read ≤ 0.1 Ω per UL 1213.

### Does this nullify certification?

The OEM manual states "any alteration to this equipment by a third party will nullify its certification." Strictly interpreted, abrading the socket bore is an "alteration." However:

- The alteration is **restoring the tool to the condition it should have been in at delivery** (i.e., bondable to ground per UL 1213 par. 22). It is corrective, not additive.
- The alteration does not change the tool's material, geometry, or function — it removes a coating from the mating surface to restore electrical continuity.
- **Document the remediation** in the DHA: "Crevice tool P/N 01768900 delivered with anodized socket bore preventing ground continuity per UL 1213 par. 22. Socket bore lightly abraded to bright metal at contact band. Post-remediation resistance: [value] Ω. DHA approved by PI and EHS on [date]."

### When to STOP and REPLACE:

If the socket bore abrasion does not achieve ≤ 0.1 Ω tool-to-wand (e.g., if the geometry prevents clean metal-to-metal contact, or if the anodize was applied after machining and there is a dimensional mismatch), **do not escalate further**. Instead, replace the tool with a confirmed-conductive crevice nozzle from a third-party ESD/EXP vacuum accessories supplier (e.g., Tiger-Vac, Ruwac, or a generic conductive aluminum crevice tool of the same bore diameter).

---

## CLAIM 6: SAFETY OF THE DIAGNOSTIC ITSELF

**Verdict: CORRECT**

Aluminum abrasion/grinding dust is itself a combustible-dust hazard — fine aluminum particles generated by abrading the tool surface are the same class of material you are trying to safely collect. The abrade-to-bright-metal test must be done:

- **BEFORE** the tool ever contacts AlSi10Mg powder.
- **Away from** any powder, powder containers, the vacuum collection bin, and any ignition sources.
- With abrasion debris captured by a **damp (IPA-dampened, not water) lint-free wipe** immediately after abrasion. The quantity of dust from lightly abrading a ~5 mm contact band is negligible (micrograms), but the principle of not creating uncontrolled combustible-dust accumulations applies (myers2013tutorialoncombustible pages 8-9).
- Wear N95 respirator and nitrile gloves during abrasion.
- Do not use power tools (grinder, Dremel) — hand abrasion with Scotch-Brite only.

---

## IMPORTANT OMISSIONS

### OMISSION A: DUST BRUSH VERIFICATION

Your procedure mentions the dust brush passed at 0.03 Ω tool-to-wand, which is good. However, you should also verify that:
1. The **brush bristles themselves** are the conductive/EXP variant (not nylon or natural fiber). Conductive bristles are typically carbon-loaded or stainless-steel wire. If the bristles are non-conductive, they can accumulate charge and produce brush discharges even though the ferrule is bonded.
2. The **ferrule-to-bristle-tip** path is conductive. Some brushes have conductive ferrules but non-conductive bristles, which creates an isolated-conductor situation at the bristle tips.

### OMISSION B: STANDARDIZED PROBE POINTS

For **repeatable** pre-use continuity checks, mark standardized probe points on each component with a small paint dot or engraving (e.g., "probe here" marks on the wand, coupler, crevice tool body, brush ferrule). This ensures that different operators measure at the same locations and that readings are comparable session-to-session. Document the expected resistance at each probe point in the SOP.

### OMISSION C: EXPECTED PER-CONNECTION RESISTANCES TABLE

Your SOP should include a table of expected per-connection resistances (as in the table in Claim 4 above) so that a student operator has a clear pass/fail reference without needing to interpret the UL 1213 standard.

### OMISSION D: GATE THE FIRST LIVE RUN ON ALL CONNECTIONS PASSING

**A single non-conforming tool should gate the entire first live run.** Do not use the crevice tool until it passes ≤ 0.1 Ω tool-to-wand. The first run can proceed with the dust brush alone (which passes), but the crevice tool must be remediated or replaced before it enters service. This is the conservative position consistent with UL 1213 par. 22 and NFPA 484 §15.3.1.1 (bruceUnknownyeartechnicalcommitteeon pages 29-32, comer2020explosionventedequipment pages 140-146).

### OMISSION E: DOCUMENT THE ANOMALY FOR NILFISK

File a formal product-quality inquiry with Nilfisk (not just a phone call) documenting: (1) the part number, (2) the measured resistance, (3) the UL 1213 par. 22 criterion, and (4) the hypothesis that the tool is anodized. Request either a replacement with a confirmed-bare or conductive-coated crevice tool, or a written engineering statement confirming that the anodize is intentional and that the tool bonds through its socket when properly seated. This creates a record that protects the lab if there is ever an audit or incident investigation.

---

## SUMMARY TABLE

| Claim | Verdict | Key Finding |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Measurement interpretation | **CORRECT** | OL/megohm is a real reading; Al₂O₃ anodize has resistivity > 10¹² Ω·cm and breakdown voltage 20–1,250 V, far above DMM test voltage; light scratches cannot penetrate Mohs 9 anodize |
| 2. Is it anodized? | **CORRECT** (most likely; no P/N documentation found) | Clear sulfuric-acid anodize matches all symptoms; alternatives eliminated; literature silent on P/N 01768900 finish |
| 3. Anodized EXP tool — defect? | **CORRECT-WITH-CAVEAT** | Anodize over grounded metal is NOT a PBD hazard (breakdown voltage ~20–125 V ≪ 4 kV PBD threshold); BUT the as-supplied socket failure to bond IS a UL 1213 non-conformance |
| 3b. As-supplied failure | **CORRECT** | Tool fails OEM's own ≤ 0.1 Ω criterion; this is non-conforming; do not use until remediated |
| 4. Governing acceptance criterion | **CORRECT-WITH-CAVEAT** | 0.1 Ω applies per metal-to-metal connection; the ~4 Ω conductive hose is a listed component with its own spec (≤ 10⁴ Ω) and does not violate the per-connection criterion |
| 5. Remediation | **CORRECT-WITH-CAVEAT** | Bond the joint (abrade socket bore to bright metal); document in DHA; if unsuccessful, replace the tool; do not strip the entire working surface |
| 6. Safety of diagnostic | **CORRECT** | Abrade before powder contact, away from ignition sources, capture debris with IPA-dampened wipe |

**Critical actions before the first live run:**
1. **Gate**: Do NOT use the crevice tool until it passes ≤ 0.1 Ω tool-to-wand. Proceed with dust brush only if needed.
2. **Diagnose**: Check for rack marks, full seating, and contact cleaner before resorting to abrasion.
3. **Remediate or replace**: Abrade socket bore per Claim 5 sequence. If unsuccessful, replace.
4. **Document**: File anomaly report with Nilfisk and record remediation in DHA.
5. **Verify brush bristles**: Confirm the dust brush has conductive (not nylon) bristles.

You are following up on a prior task: You are following up on a prior task: You are following up on a prior task: You are following up on a prior task: Context: We are setting up a Nilfisk CFM 118EXP explosion-proof industrial vacuum cleaner for collecting combustible/reactive metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg and elemental Si, typical particle size 20–63 µm with sub-micron fines). The vacuum already has, or will have installed:
- Antistatic main filter (Nilfisk PN 40000460, 99.7% @ 1.5 µm)
- Upstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631 / 1408678500, 99.97% @ 0.3 µm)
- Downstream HEPA filter (Nilfisk PN 01727631)
- OEM antistatic 1.5" hose with grounded cuffs, conductive metal wand and crevice tool, full grounding chain to building earth

Vacuum is CSA-rated Class I Group D and Class II Groups E, F, G (combustible metal dust). Spec follows NFPA 484 (Combustible Metals) and NFPA 652/660 (Combustible Dust).

The OEM Nilfisk dust collection bag (PN 107413584, the only model confirmed by a Nilfisk distributor to fit the 118EXP collection container) is paper/fleece based and not explicitly antistatic. A previous attempt to buy bags via Grainger (Nilfisk Vacuum Bag 4RYH6 fleece) was identified as non-antistatic and rejected.

Question 1 (primary): For combustible metal powder collection (AlSi10Mg, Si) in an explosion-proof industrial vacuum, is it acceptable per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 / NFPA 660 / OSHA / ATEX consensus practice to operate WITHOUT a disposable collection bag and instead rely on:
(a) the antistatic main filter + upstream HEPA + downstream HEPA already installed, AND
(b) an antistatic / conductive polyethylene liner placed inside the stainless-steel collection bin (electrically bonded to the bin / vacuum body so the grounding chain is preserved)?

Specifically address:
- Whether conductive (10^4 – 10^6 Ω surface resistivity) or static-dissipative (10^6 – 10^11 Ω) liners satisfy NFPA 484 / NFPA 652 grounding and static-control requirements for combustible metal dust collection,
- Whether the absence of a bag introduces unacceptable risks (powder fluidization, filter blinding, dust resuspension during emptying, MIE-related ignition hazards) that a bag would otherwise mitigate,
- Whether collected metal powder in a liner can be safely disposed of / transferred to an outer waste container, and what NFPA 484 says about temporary storage of reactive metal fines,
- Any documented industry guidance from Nilfisk, Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, or similar manufacturers about bag-vs-liner-vs-bagless for AlSi10Mg / aluminum / silicon powder.

Question 2 (secondary, sourcing): If a true antistatic / conductive disposable filter bag IS required (not just a liner), please identify specific commercial part numbers that:
- Fit the Nilfisk CFM 118EXP collection container (~12.5" / 320 mm internal diameter container, sized to nest in the stainless drum used on 118 EXP and A15EXP models),
- Are explicitly rated antistatic / conductive (carbon-loaded paper, conductive plastic, or antistatic-treated fleece) and suitable for combustible metal dust per NFPA 484,
- Are available from a US supplier (Nilfisk direct, Fisher Scientific, Grainger, Caliber Equipment, SweepScrub, IndustrialVacs, etc.) with a sourceable link or distributor contact.

Note that Nilfisk technical support has told us this 118EXP model is old enough that it is no longer fully supported and they cannot definitively confirm parts compatibility, so primary literature, NFPA standards interpretation, and cross-referencing alternative manufacturer (Ruwac, Tiger-Vac, VAC-U-MAX, Hafco) combustible-metal-dust accessories are particularly valuable. The serial-number sticker shows "L" prefix per Nilfisk telephone guidance.

Please cite NFPA standards by section number where possible, and provide direct product URLs for any recommended bags/liners.

3. IS AN ANODIZED EXP TOOL A DEFECT / A CONTRADICTION WITH "EXPLOSION-PROOF"? Explain the isolated-
   (ungrounded-) conductor ignition hazard (NFPA 77/484): a conductive aluminum mass insulated from ground
   can accumulate charge and produce an incendive spark. Then explain whether the hazard is resolved once
   the tool BODY is bonded to ground through a clean metal-to-metal joint — i.e., is a tens-of-micron
   anodized skin over GROUNDED metal itself an ignition concern (propagating brush discharge / coating-
   thickness thresholds), or is the only real requirement that the assembled tool not float? Is supplying
   an anodized tool consistent with an EXP-certified vacuum as long as the assembled chain bonds?

3b. AS-SUPPLIED FAILURE. Given the tool does NOT bond to the wand through its socket as supplied
   (joint reads open), is this an out-of-spec / non-conforming condition for a tool the OEM sells as part
   of an EXP-certified system whose own manual demands <= 0.1 ohm tool-to-wand before each use? What is
   the defensible course: insist on a conforming part / RMA, vs field-remediate the joint?

4. GOVERNING ACCEPTANCE CRITERION. Confirm the governing pass/fail is the OEM manual's ASSEMBLED
   tip-of-tool -> wand -> hose -> machine <= 0.1 ohm (UL 1213 par. 22), and reconcile that with the more
   permissive general NFPA 77 bonding figures (< 10 ohm for a bonded system, < 1 Mohm for static
   dissipation). Are our other readings acceptable within that chain: wand/coupler < 0.1 ohm, dust brush
   0.03 ohm, and specifically the ~4 ohm conductive hose (mfr says normal, spec R <= 10^4) — does a 4 ohm
   hose segment violate a strict 0.1-ohm-per-connection reading of the manual, and how should we treat a
   listed-conductive hose whose bulk resistance legitimately exceeds 0.1 ohm?

5. REMEDIATION. Is the correct fix to BOND THE JOINT rather than strip the tool — i.e., clean / lightly
   abrade ONLY the socket bore of the tool and the wand tip to bright metal, seat metal-to-metal, and
   re-verify <= 0.1 ohm — rather than removing the finish from the working surface? Address: (a) whether
   this counts as an "alteration that nullifies certification" and how to keep it minimal / get EHS-DHA
   sign-off; (b) non-destructive checks to try first (probe the bare masked rack-contact points left by
   anodizing; probe machined faces / cut ends that may be bare; confirm full tight seating; plastic-safe
   contact cleaner / fine non-metallic Scotch-Brite on mating surfaces only); (c) when to STOP and simply
   REPLACE it with a confirmed-conductive / ESD crevice tool instead.

6. SAFETY OF THE DIAGNOSTIC ITSELF. Aluminum abrasion/grinding dust is itself a combustible-dust hazard:
   confirm the abrade-to-bright-metal test must be done BEFORE the tool ever contacts AlSi10Mg, away from
   powder and ignition sources, with debris captured by a damp wipe, and any other controls.

Finally: list anything IMPORTANT we may be OMITTING (e.g., verifying the dust brush is the conductive-
BRISTLE EXP variant and that its ferrule path is in the continuity check; marking standardized probe
points for repeatable readings; documenting expected per-connection resistances; whether a single
non-conforming tool should gate the whole first live run). Where the literature is genuinely silent or
